And here she was: grounded.
The Traffic Light for this chapter is different — not a situation-specific guide but a self-assessment.
🟢 Grounded: You can name at least five Power-Ups and know when to use them. You’ve used at least two of them in real situations this year.
🟡 Building: You understand the Power-Ups in theory but haven’t had to use many of them yet. Keep reading. Keep the list. Your time will come — and when it does, you’ll be more ready than you think.
🔴 Struggling: You’re in a situation right now that feels bigger than your Power-Ups can handle. That’s not a failure — it’s information. Tell a trusted adult. Some situations need more than a twelve-year-old’s Power-Ups. Knowing when to call for backup is the most advanced skill in the whole book.
This chapter’s synthesis serves a specific psychological function: it consolidates scattered skills into an accessible internal framework. Research on what psychologists call “schema consolidation” shows that discrete skills taught in sequence are significantly more deployable when the learner can see their relationship to each other — when they can see the whole system.
The COMPLETE DEFENSE ARRAY isn’t just a list. It’s a cognitive map. When a child has a map, they can navigate. When they’re navigating by feel alone, even well-learned skills can be unavailable under pressure.
We suggest you read through the Power-Up list with your child, letting them explain each one in their own words. Anything they can explain, they own. Anything they can’t quite explain — that’s the skill worth revisiting.
Ask your child: “Which Power-Up have you used the most this year? Which one do you feel most ready to use? Which one feels hardest? Is there one you’ve never had to use — and do you hope you don’t, or do you feel ready?”
Build your Personal COMPLETE DEFENSE ARRAY.
Not the whole list — your list. The Power-Ups that feel most like yours. The ones you’ve actually used. The ones you think you’ll need most.
Write them on one page in your own words — not the official names if you don’t want to use them, just what they mean to you and when you’d use them.
That page lives in your journal forever. It’s your system. Take it everywhere.
Parent and child: Read through the Power-Up list together. For each one, your child explains what it is. For each one, you share whether you could have used it at some point in your own life — and what happened instead. This conversation is the whole point.
## THE POWER OF FORGIVENESS
A Guide to Forgiving Without Forgetting — And Without Leaving Yourself Behind
It’s January. Four months have passed since the first day of school, and Shaela has had time to think about most of what happened.
She’s at peace with Furbie — mostly. He did a thing, she handled it, the pen came back, the pattern is known, the relationship continues at an adjusted temperature. That’s not forgiveness exactly. That’s calibration.
She’s fine with Jumby. She learned his patterns. She doesn’t chase his drama. She genuinely likes him in the moments when he isn’t running a play. Those moments exist.
She’s wary of Fran and has adjusted her information-sharing accordingly. She doesn’t dislike Fran. She just keeps her ideas close.
She’s fully exited Amy’s orbit, amicably. Amy didn’t notice as much as Shaela expected.
And Bryant — Bryant is a separate category that she doesn’t need to resolve. She just needs to keep her Power-Ups current and her ideas private.
But there is something unresolved. Not about any of them exactly — but about a concept she’s been circling for months without quite landing on.
It’s about what to do with the weight.
Not the tricks — she’s handled those. But the feeling underneath the tricks. The confusion that Furbie’s denial created. The guilty knot from Amy’s guilt-trips. The dizzy residue from the Hot-and-Cold cycle. The strange grief of realizing the Super-Fast Best Friend was mostly engineering.
What do you do with all of that? Where does it go?
Zill says: “My grandmother calls it the carry weight. Every time someone does something that hurts, it leaves something in you. And you have a choice: carry it, or set it down. But setting it down doesn’t mean they were right. It means you don’t want to carry it anymore.”
Shaela sits with that for a long time.
This chapter’s feeling is the most complex one in the book — not a single feeling but a mixture of competing ones. The word for the overall experience of what forgiveness requires is: ready.
Not there yet. But ready to consider it. Ready to look at the carry weight and ask: does this still belong to me?
Ready is not the same as healed. It’s the feeling of being willing to look at the thing honestly and decide what to do with it from there.
#### WHAT’S THE GOAL?
Forgiveness is one of the most misunderstood words in the English language. It tends to mean different things to different people, and some of those things are not true.
What forgiveness is NOT:
- Saying what they did was okay
- Pretending it didn’t happen
- Letting them back in automatically
- Forgetting
- Being the bigger person in a way that costs you something real
- Something you have to do quickly or on someone else’s timeline
What forgiveness IS:
- Deciding not to carry the weight of what they did inside your body forever
- Releasing your grip on the anger — not because they deserve your peace, but because you do
- Being able to think about what happened without the full original pain arriving every time
- Something you do for yourself, not for them
The simplest version: forgiveness is putting something down. Not erasing it. Not endorsing it. Putting it down.
FORGIVENESS COMPASS helps you evaluate whether an apology is genuine — and whether you’re ready to receive it.
A real apology has these qualities:
- Names the behavior exactly: “I denied borrowing your pen and I did borrow it.”
- Acknowledges the impact: “That made you doubt yourself and that wasn’t fair.”
- Takes responsibility without conditions: “I’m sorry. No buts.”
- Does not demand a response on a timeline: “You don’t have to forgive me now. I just wanted you to know.”
When you receive a real apology, FORGIVENESS COMPASS asks: am I ready to put this down? You don’t have to answer immediately. The question is enough for now.
BOUNDARY ARCHITECT is the understanding that forgiveness and trust are different things — and that you can offer one without the other.
You can forgive Furbie for the pen situation — put down the weight of it — without giving him unrestricted access to your belongings again. Those are two separate decisions.
Say this
Forgiveness is internal. Boundaries are about behavior. One doesn’t cancel the other.
APOLOGY ANALYZER ELITE (upgraded from Chapter 17) runs the same test with more sophistication.
Markers of an insincere apology:
- “I’m sorry if…” — the “if” makes your pain conditional.
- “I’m sorry, but…” — the “but” transfers the responsibility back.
- “I was just joking / you’re too sensitive” — the apology turns into a critique.
- Apology given in public to manage their reputation, not to repair your relationship.
- Apology that expects an immediate forgiveness response.
When APOLOGY ANALYZER ELITE identifies an insincere apology, the move is: you don’t have to receive it. You can say “thank you” and process privately. The apology is theirs to give. What you do with it is yours.
A genuine mistake, a genuine apology, no pattern. The weight is light and the apology is real. Forgiveness feels natural and quick.
Repeated behavior, mixed apologies, genuine hurt. Forgiveness is possible but not immediate. It’s a process, not an event. You might need to put it down and pick it back up several times before it fully settles.
Someone who caused real harm, may or may not have apologized, and cannot be trusted going forward. Forgiveness here is not about the relationship — it’s entirely about you. You are releasing the weight for your own wellbeing, not because they deserve it. You can forgive a Level 3 player without having any further contact with them, without accepting their apology, and without letting them back in. The forgiveness is private. The door stays closed.
She started with the smallest one.
Furbie and the pen. Four months ago. The thing that started the whole year.
She sat with it quietly on a Tuesday afternoon and asked herself honestly: am I still carrying this?
The answer surprised her: a little. Not a lot. But a little. A small residue of the confused, doubted feeling from that moment at the water fountain.
She didn’t need Furbie to apologize. He hadn’t, and probably wouldn’t. But she could put it down anyway. She could say: this happened, it was real, I handled it, it’s done, I’m putting it down.
She wrote in her journal: Furbie and the pen. I know what happened. I trust my memory. The thing is resolved. I’m setting this down.
It was almost embarrassingly simple. A few sentences. And then something in her chest was slightly lighter.
She worked her way through the list — not to settle scores, not to assign verdicts, just to look at each carry weight and ask: does this still need to be in me?
Some did. Some weren’t ready to put down. She wrote those in a different color: not ready yet. And that’s okay.
At the end she had two lists. Things she’d set down. Things she was still working on.
Both lists were honest. That felt like the whole point.
She told Zill about it.
He was quiet for a moment. “My grandmother says forgiveness is the last Power-Up. It’s not for the other person. It’s for making sure they don’t get to live in you rent-free forever.”
Shaela laughed. “Rent-free,” she repeated.
“Exactly. You’ve already dealt with them out there.” He gestured toward the school building. “You don’t have to let them keep living in here.” He tapped his chest.
She went back to her journal that evening and wrote one more thing at the top of both pages:
The things that happened to me do not get to own me. I carry what I choose. I put down what I’m ready to put down. And I’m the one who decides.
That felt like the whole chapter. And also, she thought, like the whole year.
Research by Dr. Fred Luskin at Stanford’s Forgiveness Project, and work by Dr. Everett Worthington, consistently shows that forgiveness — defined as the release of the physiological and emotional stress response connected to a harm, not as the erasure of the event or the reconciliation of the relationship — is one of the most significant factors in long-term wellbeing. The physical health benefits of forgiveness are proven: lower cortisol, reduced blood pressure, decreased depression and anxiety.
The key distinction for children: forgiveness is not reconciliation. A child can forgive a bully without resuming friendship. A child can forgive a family member who hurt them without granting access. A child can forgive themselves for their own mistakes without minimizing the impact.
Teaching children that forgiveness is about the quality of their own internal life — not about what the other person deserves — is one of the most empowering and most practically useful things we can offer them.
Ask your child: “Is there something from this year that you’re still carrying? Do you want to put it down? What would it feel like to do that? Is there anything you need to happen first — an apology, a conversation, just time — before you’re ready?”
Start your own Carry Weight Inventory.
Write down two or three things from this year that are still in you — moments that still have some weight attached.
For each one, ask:
- Am I ready to put this down?
- If yes: write the putting-down. “This happened. I handled it. I’m setting it down.”
- If no: write “Not ready yet. And that’s okay.” Put the thing in a different color. Come back to it when you are.
There is no rush. There is no deadline. The inventory is yours. The timeline is yours.
Parent and child: Is there something you’ve been carrying from your own past — from childhood, from relationships, from things that were done to you or things you did — that you’ve put down? How did you do it? What helped? And: is there something you’re still carrying that you haven’t put down yet? You don’t have to share the specifics. But the conversation about the process — about what forgiveness actually looks and feels like from the inside — is worth having.

## THE FRIENDSHIP ARCHITECT
A Guide to Building the Best Friendships Ever
It is March, and Shaela is sitting at a lunch table with Zill, Maya, and a new kid named Remy who arrived after winter break and has turned out to be someone worth knowing.
Nobody planned this table. It just formed — the way the best things do, gradually, through a series of small choices that added up to something real. Zill had been sitting here for years. Shaela moved to this table in October when the other one stopped feeling safe. Maya had been at this table since September with an open seat she never made a thing of. Remy was new and didn’t know where to sit and Shaela said there’s space here and now, three months later, here they all are.
At some point during lunch, Remy says something that is mildly wrong about a historical fact. Zill corrects it kindly. Remy laughs and says fair enough. And they all move on in about eight seconds.
Eight seconds. From disagreement to resolution to moving on.
Shaela has spent time this year in friendships where eight seconds would have been the beginning of a whole production — where the correction would have become an accusation, where moving on would have required extensive emotional management, where she would have spent the next two hours wondering if she had done something wrong.
She looks around the table at the three people eating with her and thinks: this is what it is supposed to feel like. Not perfect. Not drama-free forever. Just: safe enough to be wrong. Safe enough to disagree and still be here at the end of it.
This is what she has been building toward.
This chapter’s feeling is different from all the others. It is not produced by something going wrong. It is the feeling of something going right.
The word for it is SAFE.
Not the absence of challenge. Not the absence of conflict. Just the presence of something exactly: a friendship where you can be completely yourself — the actual version, not the performing version — and where being imperfect does not cost you the relationship.
After a whole year of spotting tricks and running Power-Ups, this is the feeling you have been working toward.
Safe is what happens in a friendship where disagreement does not cost you the relationship, where your wins are celebrated without calculation, and where an apology, when it is needed, actually lands.
#### 🔍 What’s the trick?
There is no trick in this chapter. This chapter is the way it works — the blueprint for what real friendships look like when you build them intentionally, with the right materials.
Every chapter before this one taught you to recognize what is wrong. This chapter teaches you what right looks and feels like — so you can build it, protect it, and recognize it when you find it.
A friendship is not just the absence of tricks. It is the presence of something exactly: four building blocks that have to be there for the friendship to hold weight.
#### BUILDING BLOCK ONE: THE KINDNESS BRICK
Kindness in a real friendship is not just being pleasant when things are easy. It is being honest in a way that respects someone. It is staying warm when you disagree. It is noticing when someone needs something before they ask for it. It is the Zill move of saying fair enough and meaning it — absorbing the correction without making it a moment.
#### BUILDING BLOCK TWO: THE TRUST BRICK
Trust is not given. It is built from consistent behavior over time. Every time someone does what they said they would, the Trust Brick gets a little stronger. Every time the story matches the behavior. Every time they show up when it costs them something. Trust is the building up of small consistent things — not one grand gesture, but a hundred ordinary ones.
#### BUILDING BLOCK THREE: THE CELEBRATION BRICK
Real friends celebrate your wins without planning what they get from them. They are genuinely happy for you when something goes right — not waiting to see if your success threatens something, not adjusting their warmth based on whether your win makes them feel smaller. The Celebration Brick is what separates a friendship from a competition wearing friendship’s face.
#### BUILDING BLOCK FOUR: THE APOLOGY BRICK
The Apology Brick is the glue of the whole structure. Real friends make real apologies — exactly, without conditions, without the but that transfers responsibility back. And real friends receive apologies without weaponizing them, without storing them up, without making the apologizer perform additional contrition before being allowed back in. Both directions of the Apology Brick matter equally.
Building Block Test: Does this friendship have all four bricks?
FOUNDATION CHECK is a quiet internal audit of any friendship you are investing in. It is not suspicious — it is honest.
The questions:
- Does this friendship have genuine warmth even in hard moments? (Kindness Brick)
- Does this person do what they say they will do, the same every time? (Trust Brick)
- Is this person genuinely happy when good things happen for me? (Celebration Brick)
- When something goes wrong between us, can we repair it with a real apology? (Apology Brick)
You do not need all four bricks to be perfect. You need all four bricks to be present. A friendship missing one brick will eventually feel unstable in the specific way that missing brick predicts.
Say this
Repair Move: Using the Apology Brick when something breaks.
REPAIR PROTOCOL is the sequence for when you are the one who needs to apologize — when you have done something that damaged a friendship and you want to fix it with a real apology rather than a performance of one.
The sequence:
Name exactly what you did.
Acknowledge the impact — how it landed, not how you meant it.
Take responsibility without conditions or buts.
Ask what they need.
Then do it.
Say this
That is the whole apology. No addendum. No self-defense. No history of the other person’s wrongs attached to it.
Active Friendship Move: The Celebration Brick in practice.
CELEBRATION LAUNCH is the active, deliberate practice of being fully happy for someone else. Not performing it. Actually doing it.
When a friend succeeds at something — scores the goal, gets the grade, makes the team, finishes the project — your job is to be completely in their corner about it. No adjustment for your own feelings about the same subject. No comparison. No asterisk.
Say this
That is the whole sentence. No sequel.
This chapter does not have Trickster Levels — because there is no trick. But there are friendship levels, and knowing which one you are in helps you know what to invest and what to protect.
Level One — New and Building:
A friendship with all four bricks in early, incomplete form. Still growing. Still learning each other. The Trust Brick is just starting to accumulate. The Apology Brick has not been tested yet. This is where most friendships begin. It is a good place to be. Keep going.
Level Two — Tested and Steady:
A friendship that has all four bricks and has survived at least one hard thing. A disagreement that was repaired. A period when one of you needed more than the other could give. A moment when the friendship was tested and both people chose to stay. These friendships have weight. Invest in them.
Level Three — The Real Thing:
A friendship that has been built brick by brick over time, repaired when it cracked, celebrated consistently, and proven through repeated small honest moments that it is safe to be your actual self inside of it. These friendships are rare. When you find one — and you will — you will recognize it by the SAFE feeling. The eight-second disagreement resolution. The not having to manage yourself before you walk in.
Shaela decided she wanted to say something she had not said directly before.
She and Zill were at the bus stop after school, not talking about anything in particular, and she just said it.
“I want you to know that this year — having you to think through things with — that mattered a lot.”
Zill was quiet for a moment. Not because it was awkward. Because he was actually taking it in.
“You are easy to be honest with,” he said finally. “My grandmother says that is the rarest thing. Most people want you to be a version of yourself that is convenient for them. You never did that.”
Shaela thought about all the PATTERN SCANNER conversations, all the Power-Up sessions, all the times he had said let me think about that before saying something useful instead of something fast.
“We built something this year,” she said.
“We did,” Zill agreed.
They stood at the bus stop in comfortable silence — the kind you only get in friendships where the silence does not need to be filled. Where you can just be in the same space without performing anything at all.
Shaela did a FOUNDATION CHECK right there at the bus stop.
Kindness Brick: the way he had corrected her when she was wrong without making her feel small about it. The way he celebrated her handling of Bryant and Jumby and all of them — genuinely, without any calculation.
Trust Brick: every time he had said he would be somewhere, he was there. Every time he had said I think, he actually thought it rather than just saying what she wanted to hear.
Celebration Brick: when she had pitched the spoken word piece and it had landed, he had said that’s yours with the specific satisfaction of someone whose friend had done something real.
Apology Brick: there had been one hard week in November when Shaela had said something careless and it had landed wrong. Zill had told her directly. She had apologized specifically and without addendum. He had received it without making a record of it. The thing was done and gone.
All four bricks.
Solid.
The bus came. They got on.
“Same table next year?” she said.
He looked at her with the mild exasperation of someone being asked whether water is wet.
“Obviously same table,” he said.
The four building blocks in this chapter map directly to what relationship researchers call the key dimensions of secure attachment and healthy connection: warmth and attunement (Kindness Brick), reliability and safety (Trust Brick), delight in the other person’s success (Celebration Brick), and the rupture-repair cycle (Apology Brick). These four dimensions appear consistently across adult relationship research as the markers of what psychologists call “secure” relationships — connections where both people feel genuinely safe.
The ability to identify what a healthy relationship feels like from the inside is one of the most protective things a child can develop. Children who can name what is right — not just what is wrong — are much better equipped to seek it out, build it intentionally, and recognize its absence.
Worth noting: the Celebration Brick is the one most often missing in adult relationships. We have been taught to say congratulations, but genuine delight in someone else’s success — with no adjustment for our own feelings, no competitive recalculation — is a practice that requires conscious attention. Modeling it for your child when they succeed is one of the most important things you can do.
Ask your child: “What are the three friendships in your life where you feel most like yourself? What do those friendships have that others do not? Which of the four building blocks feels strongest in each one — and which one could be stronger?”

Write down what would make the lowest-scoring brick one point higher.

And: what is one building block you want to get better at offering in your own friendships — not just to your child’s friends, but to the people in your own life?
## QUIET HEROES
A Guide to Everyday Bravery and Standing Up
It is April, and Shaela is in the hallway when she sees it happen.
Remy — the new kid from winter break, now fully a person Shaela cares about — is standing at their locker when Jumby walks past and makes a comment about Remy’s shoes. Not loud. Just loud enough for the people nearby to hear. Loud enough to produce the three-second laugh from the cluster of kids around Jumby that he had aimed for.
Remy’s face does something small and controlled. The practiced neutrality of someone who has learned that reacting gives the other person exactly what they want.
The three seconds happen.
Shaela is standing eight feet away. She feels the familiar pull toward staying quiet. The math that runs automatically: this is not my fight, I was not the target, getting involved might make it about me, Remy seems fine, maybe I am overreacting.
She has run this math before. She knows what it makes. Nothing. The math makes nothing except the low-grade sick feeling of having seen something and said nothing. Of being complicit in the way Chapter 21 described — not because she meant to be, but because silence felt safer than speaking.
She takes one breath.
“Hey Jumby,” she says. Normal tone. Not loud. Not dramatic. “That was not a great thing to say.”
Jumby turns around with the mildly surprised look of someone who expected silence. “I was just joking.”
“Still not that great.” She turns to Remy. “Cool shoes, actually.”
She keeps walking.
The hallway does not part. Nobody applauds. Jumby does not have a revelation. Remy gives her a small nod — the nod of someone who noticed that someone saw them.
That nod.
That is the whole thing.
This chapter’s feeling is not produced by something going wrong to you. It is produced by standing at the edge of something brave. The feeling just before the sentence. The moment between seeing and speaking.
The word for it is READY.
Not fearless. Not certain about the outcome. Not sure it will go well. Just: willing. The door is in front of you and you know how to open it.
Ready in this context is the feeling of doing something brave not because the fear is gone but because the right thing is bigger than the scared thing.
#### 🔍 What’s the trick?
There is no trick in this chapter either.
This chapter is about the gap — the specific two-second gap between seeing something wrong and doing something about it. And the particular kind of courage it takes to close that gap.
Researchers call people who close the gap active bystanders. In every study of bullying, harassment, and social cruelty, the single most powerful variable in whether the behavior continues or stops is whether someone nearby speaks up. Not confronts dramatically. Not fights back. Just: says something.
The research finding is consistent and striking: when one person speaks, the behavior stops within ten seconds more than half the time. One sentence. Said by one person. Changes what happens next more than fifty percent of the time.
Here is what makes the gap hard to close:
THE person watching FREEZE: The moment of seeing something wrong and running the mental math of whether to act. The math is almost always biased toward inaction. This is not because people are cowards — it is because the brain, under social pressure, defaults to the option that requires the least risk. The freeze is human. The question is whether the right thing can outweigh the scared thing.
THE WHAT WILL THEY THINK FEAR: The fear that speaking up will make you look weird, too earnest, like a target, like you are making too big a deal of something. This fear is particularly strong in middle childhood and early adolescence, when social perception feels like survival.
Here is what the research also shows about that fear: the people who speak up are generally respected more afterward, not less — including by the people who laughed. The person watching who says hey, that was not cool changes the social meaning of the moment. What was a shared laugh becomes something that one person named as wrong. The namer gets credit, even from people who did not name it themselves.
Move #1: Seeing something wrong and staying quiet.
BRAVE VOICE is the smallest possible unit of intervention: one sentence, said normally, without drama.
It does not have to be a speech. It does not have to be clever. It does not have to change everything.
Say this
- “Hey, that was not cool.”
- “That was a rough thing to say.”
- “Are you okay?” (said to the person who was targeted)
- “That is not true about them.”
The sentence does not fix everything. It changes the temperature of the room by one degree. One degree is enough to matter.
What BRAVE VOICE does not require: perfect words, certainty of outcome, fearlessness, or an audience. BRAVE VOICE can be one sentence said quietly to one person. It counts.
Move #2: Wanting to help but missing the moment in real time.
SIDE DOOR SUPPORT is the private, after-the-fact version of BRAVE VOICE. Sometimes the moment passes before you can say anything in public. Sometimes the situation is too charged. Sometimes you did not catch it until it was over.
SIDE DOOR SUPPORT is finding the person afterward and saying: “I saw that. I want you to know I did not think it was okay. Are you alright?”
This is sometimes more important than the public move. The person being targeted does not always need the public correction. They need to know that someone saw them — that they were not invisible, that the thing that happened was witnessed and named, that they are not alone in having noticed it was wrong.
Say this
Move #3: The What Will They Think Fear is loudest.
INNER CHAMPION is the internal speech for the moment when the fear of social what happens next is louder than anything else.
Say this
INNER CHAMPION is not a performance. It is a private alignment between who you are and what you do in the moments when nobody is watching how you feel — only what you choose.
This chapter does not have Trickster Levels for a Tricky Player. It has bravery levels.
Level One — Low Stakes Practice:
You see something small and slightly unkind in a low-pressure setting. The social cost of speaking is minimal. This is where you practice BRAVE VOICE — not when everything is on the line, but when the risk is small and the reps are building your confidence. Use Level One situations to practice. When the Level Three moment comes, the sentence will already be in your mouth.
Level Two — Social Cost Present:
You see something clearly wrong and the person doing it has social power — popularity, a group around them, status you do not have. BRAVE VOICE feels risky here. The math says stay quiet. Use it anyway. The sentence you need is short. The risk is usually smaller than the math says.
Level Three — The Full Moment:
You see something serious — going on for a while cruelty, organized exclusion, something that is genuinely harming someone. One sentence in the moment may not be enough. The full sequence here is: BRAVE VOICE in the moment + SIDE DOOR SUPPORT for the person targeted + telling a trusted adult. You do not have to fix it alone. You just have to be the one who says something and gets the people who can do more involved.
Remy found Shaela after school by the side door.
“Thanks,” Remy said. “For the hallway thing.”
“It was nothing.”
“It was not nothing.” Remy said it simply, without drama. “I have been in schools where nobody says anything. Ever. And you get used to it. You figure that is just how it is.”
“It does not have to be,” Shaela said.
“I know that now.” A pause. “My first week here I thought you and Zill were just being nice because I was new. Like it would wear off.”
“Did it wear off?”
“No.” Remy looked at her with the specific expression of someone who is genuinely surprised and has decided to let the surprise be a good thing. “That is the thing. It did not.”
They walked to the corner where their routes home split. Shaela looked at Remy’s shoes. They were genuinely interesting — a very specific kind of interesting that only made sense once you knew something about who Remy was. Distinct and considered and a little bit unexpected, the way Remy was.
“Cool shoes,” Shaela said again.
Remy laughed. “You already said that.”
“I meant it both times.”
She walked home thinking about what BRAVE VOICE had actually done that afternoon. Not fixed Jumby — he would find another target and another comment. Not ended cruelty in the hallway — that would require a whole system to change. Just: made one person’s afternoon one degree less alone. Made it so that one person went home knowing they had been seen.
One degree.
She thought about the research on person watching intervention that Zill had read to her once — how one person speaking stops the behavior more than half the time. How the loudest silence is the one right before the first person says something. How that first person is almost always someone who had been quiet before and decided, this time, to do it differently.
She had been that person today.
INNER CHAMPION had done the rest.
Research by Dr. Wendy Craig and Dr. Debra Pepler found that in roughly eighty-five percent of bullying incidents, peers were present. In those incidents, peer intervention stopped the bullying within ten seconds in fifty-seven percent of cases. One sentence from one person changes the outcome more than half the time.
Teaching children to be active bystanders — not heroes, not vigilantes, just people who say one sentence — is one of the most evidence-based interventions in bullying prevention research. The gap between seeing and speaking is bridged by practice. Children who have practiced BRAVE VOICE at low stakes deploy it more readily at high stakes. This is a skill that improves with repetition, which means the best time to practice it is now, in small moments, before the large ones arrive.
The most important thing you can do alongside this chapter: share your own story. The moment you wish you had spoken up and did not. The time you did, and what happened. The version of yourself you are proud of in a hard moment. Your honesty about the gap between seeing and speaking makes your child’s honesty possible.
Ask your child: “Can you think of a time when you saw something wrong and did not say anything? What stopped you? What do you wish you had said? And then — can you think of a time when you did say something, even something small? What happened? How did it feel?”
This week, practice BRAVE VOICE once.
It does not have to be a dramatic situation. Find one moment — any moment — where one sentence from you would be the right thing to say. It might be as small as “That is not true about them” or “Are you okay?” or “Hey, that was a bit rough.”
Say it. One sentence. Said normally.
Then notice what happens in the room. And notice what happens inside you.
Write both things down.
Parent and child: Tell each other about a moment when you wish you had said something and did not. What stopped you? What do you wish you had done? And then tell each other about a moment when you did say something — however small. What happened? How did it feel afterward compared to the times you stayed quiet?
## THE KINDNESS CHAIN REACTION
A Guide to How One Good Thing Grows
Tuesday. Shaela is running slightly late and she almost walks past the situation entirely.
But she does not.
A younger kid — sixth grade, she thinks, she does not know them — is standing outside the cafeteria with a lunch tray and an expression of pure social paralysis. Every table has the visible territorial quality of established groups, and this kid is standing at the entrance doing the calculation of options that do not look great.
Shaela has approximately thirty seconds of her own lunch period to spare.
“Hey,” she says. “There is space at our table.”
The kid — whose name turns out to be Kai — looks at her with the specific wariness of someone who has been on the receiving end of apparent kindness that turned out to be something else. “Really?”
“Yeah. Come on.”
They sit down. Zill makes room without making a thing of it. Remy asks what Kai’s name is and then asks a follow-up question about the answer, which is the social move that turns an introduction into a conversation. Maya offers half of an ongoing discussion about a show they both apparently watch.
Twenty minutes later Kai leaves the cafeteria looking like a different person than the one who had been paralyzed at the entrance.
The next day Shaela sees Kai hold a door open for three people in a row — with the specifically generous energy of someone who has just been on the receiving end of something good and is passing it on without quite knowing they are doing it.
She does not say anything. She does not need to.
She just watches the chain continue without her.
The Kindness Chain Reaction makes a feeling that is different from almost every other chapter in this book. It is not produced by a trick. It is not the relief of having used a Power-Up correctly. It is the warm, slightly expanding feeling of having done something good without a strategy behind it.
The word for it is CONNECTED.
Not connected to a specific person, exactly — though that is part of it. Connected to something larger than yourself. To the fact that what you do moves into the world and keeps moving, in ways you will never fully track, and that this movement matters even when you cannot see it.
Connected is what happens when you do something kind without a receipt attached to it, and feel — genuinely, in your chest — that you are part of something larger than yourself.
#### 🔍 What’s the trick?
There is no trick in this chapter. This chapter is about what happens when you stop running defense against the world and start contributing to it.
The Kindness Chain Reaction is real and it is proven. Prosocial behavior is contagious in a measurable way. When people experience genuine kindness, they are a lot more likely to extend it — to different people, in different contexts, sometimes hours or days later. Researchers call this phenomenon moral elevation: the warm, expanding feeling that comes from witnessing or receiving genuine goodness, which then motivates the witness to act similarly.
The chain does not require you to see it. The chain does not require you to be thanked for starting it. The chain happens because you acted, and the action travels forward into the world in ways you will never fully map.
Here is what the Kindness Chain Reaction requires:
It requires specificity. Generic niceness is noticed but does not land the same way as specific kindness. There is space at our table is different from there is space somewhere. It is aimed at Kai, for a reason Shaela could see. specific kindness lands because it says: I saw you exactly. I responded to you exactly.
It requires no audience. The kindness done when only the recipient knows is worth more, not less. The point is the person, not the performance. If you are looking around to see who noticed, the kindness has changed into something else.
It requires no trade. The kindness with no invoice, no expectation of return, no social credit being mentally tracked — this is the purest fuel for the chain reaction. The moment a favor is expected back, the kindness becomes an investment. Investments can return value. But only gifts travel.
Move #1: Finding something to give without a strategy.
KINDNESS BOOMERANG is the practice of giving something — your time, a seat, a compliment, your attention, a true piece of information — with no expectation of return and no tracking of whether it comes back.
Give it. Then let it go. Do not monitor what happens. Do not check whether it was received the way you meant it. Do not tally whether you are ahead or behind in the relationship’s informal ledger.
The boomerang does come back. But not necessarily to you, and not necessarily from the same person, and not necessarily in a form you will recognize. That is the point. The chain travels in directions you cannot predict.
Practice: “What is one thing I can give today — freely, without a receipt?” Then give it and genuinely let it go.
Move #2: Making the kindness specific rather than general.
SPECIFIC NOTICING is the practice of naming the specific thing you see rather than delivering a generic compliment or a general warmth.
The difference:
- Generic: “Good job today.”
- exactly: “I noticed you stayed and helped clean up even when most people had already left. That mattered.”
The specific version lands because it proves you were actually paying attention. It says: I saw the real thing, not just the surface of the thing. People can feel the difference between being seen and being generically acknowledged.
Practice: Before you compliment someone, find the specific true thing. Then say that instead of the general version.
Move #3: Recognizing that your small action is the beginning of something.
RIPPLE EFFECT is a way of thinking about your actions — not just their immediate consequence but their travel. A stone dropped in water creates rings that move outward long after the stone has sunk. Your kindness works the same way.
This is not about being grandiose about small things. It is about not dismissing small things as too small to matter. The door you held, the seat you made room for, the sentence you said when you saw something wrong — these move outward in ways you will not always see.
Internal reminder: “I started something. I do not need to watch it travel. It travels anyway.”
This chapter’s levels are not about tricky players — they are about the three scales at which the Kindness Chain Reaction can operate.
Level One — The without planning it Act:
A random act of kindness with no history behind it. Holding a door. Helping someone pick something up. Noticing someone standing alone and standing near them. No relationship required. Just the moment and the response to it. This is where the chain begins.
Level Two — The going on for a while Practice:
Kindness in an existing relationship — celebrating a friend’s win with full genuine enthusiasm, repairing something before being asked to, showing up when you did not have to. The four building blocks from Chapter 25 in active practice. This is the kindness that builds foundations over time.
Level Three — The Structural Act:
Building something that creates the conditions for kindness to happen regularly. Starting a table where new people know they are welcome. Building a culture in a classroom, a team, or a group where the standard is raised — where people expect to be treated with basic dignity because that is just how this group operates. This takes more time and more ongoing effort. It is also more powerful. The chain does not just continue — it accelerates.
Zill had a theory about the chain reaction that he shared at the bus stop.
“My grandmother says kindness is lazy when it only goes to people who have already been kind to you,” he said. “The real version goes to people who have not earned it yet. Who might not even recognize it when it comes.”
“That sounds harder,” Shaela said.
“It is. But it is also the only version that travels.” He paused. “Think about Kai. You did not know Kai. Kai had not done anything for you. You made room because Kai was standing there and needed room. That is the pure version.”
Shaela thought about it. “What if Kai had been strange or difficult?”
“Then it would have been even more important.” He smiled slightly. “The kindness that only goes to people who are easy to be kind to is just preference with a nicer name.”
She sat with that for a long time.
She thought about all the Power-Ups from the year — all the defensive moves, the shields, the exits, the scanners. They had been necessary. She had needed all of them.
But sitting here watching Kai hold a door for three people in a row, she thought maybe the defensive system was the prerequisite. The thing that kept you safe enough to do the actual work.
The actual work was contributing something. Not protecting yourself from the world — giving something to it.
“Kindness is the offensive game,” she said.
Zill looked at her. “Explain.”
“All year we have been playing defense. Spotting tricks, running Power-Ups, protecting the perimeter. That is necessary. But defense is not the whole game. At some point you have to score.”
Zill considered this seriously, the way he considered everything that deserved it. “You are saying the Kindness Chain Reaction is the scoring.”
“I am saying if you only play defense, the best outcome is nothing bad happens. But nothing good happening is its own kind of loss.”
He nodded slowly. “My grandmother is going to love you when she meets you.”
Shaela laughed. “She already sounds like someone I would learn a lot from.”
“She would say the same about you.”
The chain reaction, she thought, was already happening. Right here. Between two people who had built something worth having and were, in this moment, adding to it without any calculation at all.
Research by Jonathan Haidt at NYU on moral elevation — the emotion triggered by witnessing acts of virtue or kindness — shows consistent physiological responses: a warm, expanding sensation in the chest, increased desire to help others, and measurable increases in prosocial behavior in the hours following the witnessing. The chain reaction in this chapter is not metaphorical. It is physiologically documented.
For children, the most powerful modeling you can do is not lecturing about kindness but performing it visibly, specifically, and without expectation of return — and allowing your child to witness it. The acts of kindness they see you perform for people who can do nothing for you will shape their default orientation toward the world more than any conversation about why kindness matters.
Zill’s grandmother’s observation — that kindness is lazy when it only goes to people who have already earned it — is worth sitting with. Most people are kind to people they like. The harder and more important practice is kindness extended to people on the margins of your attention: the new kid, the person who is not performing well enough to deserve it, the one who has not yet done anything for you. That is the version of kindness that actually travels.
Ask your child: “What is the most specific act of kindness anyone has ever shown you — not a big gift, just a small moment where someone noticed something and responded to it? How did it feel? Did it change how you acted toward others afterward? And: is there a Kai in your school right now — someone standing at the entrance of the cafeteria calculating their options? What would it take to say there is space at our table?”
This week, start a Kindness Chain.
Each day for five days, do one specific act of kindness with no expectation of return. Specific means: aimed at a particular person, for a particular reason you have actually noticed about them. Not generic. Not performed. Just: you saw something, and you responded to it.
At the end of five days, write down:
- What you did each day
- What you noticed (about the person, about yourself)
- Whether you saw any ripple effect
You do not need a ripple effect to have succeeded. The giving was the success. The ripple, if it comes, is the bonus.
Parent and child: Tell each other about someone who was specifically kind to you — not in a big planned way, but in a small noticed way. What did they see in you that made the kindness specific and real? And then: what is one act of kindness you want to do this week — for someone who has not necessarily earned it yet, who might not even recognize it when it comes? Plan it together and report back.
## THE FINAL LEVEL
A Celebration of How Far You Have Come
It is May. The school year is almost over.
Shaela is at her locker — the same locker she was standing at in September when Furbie told her the pen never happened and the floor had shifted under her feet — and she is thinking about the list.
Not the Power-Up list, though that is part of it. Not the Trickster list, though that is part of it too. The other list. The one she made in January in the library when she was trying to understand what she knew now that she had not known in September.
She knows what the Memory Mixer-Upper is, and she knows that the confused, floor-shifting feeling it makes is the trick working — not evidence that she is wrong.
She knows how to separate someone’s feelings from someone’s choices, and she knows that the Blame Game puts both in the same pile and tries to hand them to her.
She knows how guilt is installed and how to distinguish the real kind — the useful kind, the kind that says I did something wrong and I want to fix it — from the fake obligation kind that arrives pre-packaged from someone else’s need.
She knows the difference between a friendship that floods with intensity to bypass her judgment and a friendship that builds in layers because it actually has something to build.
She knows the SAFE feeling from the inside now. Not just as a concept. As a felt thing. As something she can locate in her chest when she is at the table with Zill and Remy and Maya and things are as they should be.
She knows how to go direct, broadcast truth, scramble a signal, and perform a clean exit. She knows how to stay on the ground when someone tries to put her on a pedestal. She knows how to play boring against someone who needs her reaction as fuel.
She knows that the Mean Voice in her head is installed content, not original content, and that it can be argued with using receipts. She knows how to forgive without forgetting and how to put down carry weight when she is ready to put it down.
And she knows — maybe most importantly — what the chain reaction of kindness feels like when it is running. The warm-chest CONNECTED feeling of having given something freely and watched it travel without needing to follow it.
She closes the locker.
She is ready for whatever comes next.
This chapter’s feeling is the most complete one in the book. It is not produced by a single event. It is produced by the building up of everything — all the chapters, all the Power-Ups, all the conversations, all the hard moments that turned into skills.
The word for it is WHOLE.
Not finished. Not perfect. Not past difficulty. Just: more complete than you were. In possession of something that belongs to you now. The vocabulary, the tools, the map, the feeling of safe from the inside — these live in you now in a way they did not in September.
Whole does not mean fixed or finished. It means more complete than you were. In possession of something you did not have before.
#### WHAT’S THE GOAL?
This chapter is not a lesson. It is a ceremony.
You made it through twenty-eight chapters of tricks and Power-Ups and Trickster Levels and stories and Traffic Lights and quests and conversations with the people who love you. That is not nothing. That is a year of learning that most people do not get until they are much older — and some people never get at all.
Let us take stock of what you now have:
You have 28 Power-Ups. You know when to use each one. You have practiced at least some of them in real situations, which means they live in your hands now and not just your head.
You have a Feeling Vocabulary with 28 words for 28 specific emotional experiences. The next time something happens, you can name it within seconds instead of carrying an unnamed thing in your stomach for days.
You have the Traffic Light system — so you know when to handle something yourself, when to loop in an adult, and when to get help immediately. That decision framework, practiced over 28 chapters, is now automatic.
You have the Grown-Up Corner relationship with the adult who read this with you — which means you have at least one person who has been reading the same book, building the same vocabulary, learning the same names for the same things. That shared language is one of the most valuable things this book created.
And you have the four building blocks for real friendship: Kindness, Trust, Celebration, and Apology. Which means you know how to build something worth having and you know what it feels like from the inside when you have found it.
What does a Playground Protector actually do?
They notice. They name what they notice. They respond with the right tool. They stay steady when things are uncertain. They go direct when information is being filtered. They protect their own memory, their own feelings, their own choices. They give kindness without a receipt. They say something when something is wrong. They build friendships with all four bricks. They put down what they are ready to put down and hold on to what they are not yet ready to release. They trust their INNER GPS. They run COURAGE SURGE when the right thing is scary.
And when they get confused — which still happens, because it always happens to everyone — they take one breath, name what is happening, and pick one Power-Up. Not the perfect one. Just one. Any one. And they go from there.
That is the whole job.
You have got it.
Reflection Move: Checking in with your complete system.
THE FULL INVENTORY is a practice, not a one-time event. Once a season — or whenever you feel like you have drifted from your grounding — go through your Power-Up Master Guide in the back of this book and check in.
Which Power-Ups have you used? Which ones do you feel most ready for? Which ones do you hope you never need? Which ones do you currently have a situation where you need them?
The inventory is not a test. It is a check-in with yourself. The map does not expire. It just updates.
Teaching Move: Passing it on.
TEACH IT FORWARD is one of the most effective ways to know you have actually learned something: explain it to someone else. Find one person — a younger sibling, a friend, a cousin, someone new to your school — who could use one Power-Up you have learned.
Do not lecture. Have a conversation. Start with: “Something happened to me once, and here is what I figured out.”
Teaching something is the deepest way to know you have it. If you can say it in your own words to someone who needs it, it is yours.
Commitment Move: The Playground Protectors Pledge.
See the full Playground Protectors Pledge in the back of this book.
Read it out loud. Sign it. You can do it alone or with someone. Either way, the saying of it makes it real in a way the reading of it does not quite. Saying something out loud is the oldest form of commitment we have. Use it.
This chapter’s levels are about where you are right now, at the end of the journey.
Level One — You Have the Map:
You have read the book and understood the concepts. You have the vocabulary. You have the Power-Up names. You have the framework. You are ready to start applying it in real situations. The map is in your hands. Now you start walking with it.
Level Two — You Are Using the System:
You have used several Power-Ups in real situations this year. You have made some of them yours — they come naturally now, without having to look them up. You have had at least one conversation with a trusted adult using the shared vocabulary this book built. You are not just a reader. You are a practitioner.
Level Three — You Are Teaching It:
You have used the system, taught something from it to at least one other person, and had real conversations — with a parent, with a friend, with anyone — where the vocabulary made something speakable that was not speakable before. At Level Three you are not just protecting yourself. You are expanding the circle of people who have the tools.
Zill found her at the locker.
“Last week,” he said.
“Last week,” she confirmed.
They walked toward homeroom in the comfortable rhythm of people who have been walking the same direction together for a long time.
“What is the thing you are taking with you?” Zill asked.
It was the kind of question he asked — the one that seemed simple and was not. The one that required actual thought rather than a fast answer.
She thought about it seriously. Not about what she was supposed to say. About what was actually true.
“I trust what I actually know,” she said finally. “That is the main one. Before this year I was so easy to confuse. Someone would tell me I remembered something wrong and I would start doubting. Someone would manufacture intensity and I would mistake it for depth. Someone would use guilt and I would carry it as if it were mine.” She paused. “I trust what I actually know now. That is the core thing. Everything else is built on top of it.”
Zill nodded. “For me it is the Pattern Scanner. Not panicking at one incident. Looking for the pattern. Because the pattern is the truth, not the incident.”
“Your grandmother taught you that?”
“She taught me a version of it. You would be surprised how much of what I have said this year is basically her, translated slightly.”
“Tell her I said thank you.”
“She already knows about you,” Zill said. “She said: the girl who holds her ground sounds like someone who has been doing the work.”
Shaela smiled. “She would say that about a lot of people.”
“She would,” Zill agreed. “But she said it specifically about you.”
They turned the corner toward homeroom.
Shaela thought about the year — Furbie and the pen, Jumby and the chips, Amy and the Super-Fast Best Friend, Bryant and all his careful engineering, Fran and her partial secrets, the group chat and the single sentence that shifted the temperature, Remy at the cafeteria entrance, Kai and the door held open for three people in a row.
All of it had been real. All of it had cost something. And all of it had produced something — tools she had not had before, skills that lived in her hands now, a friend who asked the real questions and waited for the real answers.
“Hey,” she said at the homeroom door. “Next year — same table at lunch?”
Zill looked at her with the mild exasperation of someone being asked whether water is wet.
“Obviously,” he said. “Same table.”
She walked in.
She was ready.
You have now read twenty-eight chapters of a children’s book about psychological manipulation and relational protection. Some of it — perhaps more than you expected — was about your own life too.
This chapter is an invitation: carry the conversation forward. The vocabulary you built together — the Power-Ups, the Trickster Levels, the Feeling Words, the Traffic Light — does not belong only to the book. It belongs to your relationship with your child now. Use it. When something happens at school, ask: “Which Power-Up would you use?” When you see your child navigating something difficult, name what you see: “That looks like the Pattern Scanner in action.” When you see them do something brave — especially the small moves, the one-sentence moves, the quiet BRAVE VOICE moments — name it: “That was BRAVE VOICE. I saw it.”
And when you encounter the same patterns in your own adult life — which you will, because these patterns do not stop at graduation — tell your child about it. Tell them you ran into a Blame Game situation at work. Tell them you recognized the Hot-and-Cold cycle in an adult relationship and used Steady Sunshine. Tell them you used COURAGE SURGE when something needed to be said and the scared thing was very loud.
Your transparency normalizes theirs. Your using the vocabulary keeps it alive. Your honesty about the moments when you did not have the tools — and what happened then — is the most powerful teaching you can offer.
The book ends here. The work does not.
Ask your child: “What is the thing you are taking from this year — from this book — that you will still have when you are my age? What do you want to carry forward? And what do you want to put down?” Then tell them what you are taking forward too — and what you are putting down.
Your final quest has three parts. All three matter.
Part One: Your Personal Power-Up Inventory.
Write down the five Power-Ups you feel most ready to use. Not the ones you think you should feel ready for — the ones that feel genuinely yours now. In your own words: what they are, when you would use them, and what the script sounds like when you say it.
Part Two: Teach It Forward.
Find one person who could use one Power-Up you have learned. Not a lecture — a conversation that starts: “Something happened to me once, and here is what I figured out.” See what happens.
Part Three: Take the Pledge.
Turn to the Playground Protectors Pledge in the back of this book. Read it out loud. Both the child version and — if your grown-up is there — the parent version together. Then sign it.
You have earned this. Go take it.
Parent and child: Do the Playground Protectors Pledge together. Out loud. Both of you. Read every word. Then: put this book down and look at each other. Tell each other one thing you learned. Tell each other one thing you want to do differently. Tell each other one thing you are proud of in the other person.
That conversation is the whole point.
That conversation is what the book was for.

Gives a compliment so specific it actually lands.
## The Trickster’s Glossary
When someone says "that didn't happen" to make you doubt your own memory. The confused feeling is the trick working — not a sign that you're wrong.
When someone makes a choice and hands all the bad feelings to you instead of owning it themselves. Your feelings are real — but their choices belong to them.
When guilt — real or made-up — is used to get you to do something you wouldn't normally do. Caring about someone and saying no to them are not opposites.
When someone rushes a friendship — lots of texts, "you're my ONLY friend," jealousy if you talk to others — all before you even really know them. Real friendship grows over time.
When someone uses silence and being ignored like a punishment to make you feel guilty. The silence is the trick, not a verdict about who you are.
Using gossip, rumors, and whispers to turn friends against each other. The person starting the whispers stays hidden while you deal with the mess.
Switching between being super warm and super cold — unpredictably — to keep you guessing and working hard to get back the warmth. The warmth feels better BECAUSE of how cold the cold is. That's on purpose.
Using jealousy to push between you and your friends — shrinking your world slowly while making their share bigger.
Wrapping a put-down inside a compliment — "You're good, but Jake is better" — so the sting arrives without warning.
Dropping half-information that creates worry and then walking away — so you're upset about something you can't even address. Drama is how they stay important.
Using "everyone is doing it" to make your own choices feel wrong. The activity isn't the point — getting you to go along is.
Copying your movements and matching your energy on purpose, to make you feel a bond before you've actually built one — then using that trust to get what they want.
Giving you a compliment and then using it as a reason you owe them something. The compliment was an investment, not a gift.
Using secrets as tools — sharing just enough to worry you, but not enough for you to do anything about it. Heavy secrets need grown-ups, not just you.
Using scary warnings — always delivered as "just letting you know" — to stop you from doing the right thing. The threat is almost always bigger than the real consequence.
Moving a whole group's opinion against you — quietly, invisibly — so you never know who to address. The answer is to put your truth out there directly.
The buildup and teardown cycle: shower you with warmth → pull it away when you do anything "wrong" → warm you back up → repeat. The warmth was real. The speed was the strategy.
What Level 3 Tricky Players do: they watch without showing it, they don't really care about your feelings (they just track them like data), and they plan moves way in advance. The answer: become boring to them.
A group that uses the fear of being kicked out to control what you think, say, and do. Healthy groups let you leave freely. That's the most important test.
Someone online who isn't who they say they are — building your trust before asking for personal information or a meeting. Always verify. Always video-call first.
Using group chats, screenshots, and online pile-ons to hurt someone while keeping deniability. One sentence from one person changes things more than half the time.
The inner critic — built from things other people have said — that arrives in your own voice and tries to take away good moments. It hates evidence. Collect receipts.
Your full system of 28+ Power-Ups, organized into Perception (spotting), Response (acting), and Recovery (healing). When in doubt: one breath, name the trick, pick any one Power-Up.
Putting down the weight of something that was done to you — not because they deserve your peace, but because you do. Forgiving doesn't mean forgetting or letting them back in.
Building real friendships with four bricks: Kindness, Trust, Celebration, and Real Apologies. All four need to be present — even just a little — for the friendship to hold.
Choosing to say one sentence when you see something wrong. One sentence from one person stops the bad thing more than half the time. You don't have to be loud. You just have to say something.
When kindness given freely — with no receipt and no audience — travels into the world and keeps growing in ways you can't track. Give the boomerang. Then let it go.
The last chapter and the biggest one: you've earned 28+ Power-Ups, a full Feeling Vocabulary, the four building blocks of friendship, and the knowledge of what SAFE feels like from the inside. You're ready.
## The Feeling Words Index
Twenty-eight words for twenty-eight experiences. When you can’t name the feeling — find it here.
The spinning "wait, did I make that up?" feeling when someone tries to twist your memory.
When you get blamed for someone else's choices and there was no version of what you did that would have been okay.
The heavy feeling of owing something you never agreed to owe.
When a friendship moves faster than you can keep up — and slowing down feels dangerous.
When someone removes you from their world without explaining why.
Being talked about without being talked to. Being a topic in someone else's conversation about your own life.
Off-balance because someone keeps switching between warm and cold — so you're always tracking the temperature.
When someone pushes into the space between you and someone you care about.
The quiet shrinking that happens when criticism is hidden inside a compliment.
The low-level worry of a problem you can't solve because it's not specific enough to address.
When it feels like everyone has already decided — and you're the only one who hasn't agreed yet.
When you realize the safe feeling you had was set up on purpose.
When someone's kindness turns out to be a trade you didn't know you were agreeing to.
(Information) Holding a secret that's too much to ignore and not enough to act on.
When fear arrives specific enough that your body wants to stay very still.
Being in the room — but not in the conversation. Present for a decision that was made without you.
The feeling of having been very high very fast — and then very low very fast.
The cold-but-useful feeling when all the confusing pieces finally form a pattern.
When a group's rules start feeling less like structure and more like a grip.
When something feels real and also doesn't quite add up — and you're not sure which signal to trust.
The uncomfortable feeling of having seen something wrong and stayed quiet.
Self-directed — when your own inside voice starts doing the work of every Tricky Player combined.
When all the skills you've built settle into your body as actual knowing — not just theory.
Not healed yet. Not certain. Just: willing to look at the thing and decide what to do with it.
The feeling in a friendship where you can be your full, real self — and being imperfect doesn't cost you the relationship.
(Brave) Standing at the edge of something brave. Not fearless. Just: willing.
The warm-chest feeling of having given something freely and being part of something larger than yourself.
More complete than you were. In possession of something you didn't have before.
## The big ideas, on one page each
Flip here any time you need a quick reminder of how it all works.
### 🧭 The Protector’s Method
Every trick in this book is beaten with the same four steps.
### 💚 Real Friend vs 💔 Tricky Person
When you’re not sure about someone, check the list.
- Is happy when good things happen to you
- Remembers things the way they really happened
- Says sorry and means it
- Likes you the same on good days and bad days
- Lets you say no and still stays your friend
- Makes you feel bigger
- Gets jealous or competes when you win
- Rewrites what happened until you doubt yourself
- Says sorry to end the talk, then does it again
- Is warm one day and cold the next
- Punishes you with silence when you say no
- Makes you feel smaller
One bad day doesn’t make someone tricky. A pattern does.
### 📊 The Trickster Level Meter
Tricks come in sizes. Knowing the size tells you what to do.
### 🚦 Can I handle this — or is it grown-up time?
## The Playground Protectors Pledge
I am a Playground Protector.
I trust what I actually know — even when someone tries to make me doubt it.
I take what is mine and only what is mine. I do not carry other people's choices or fake guilt.
I build friendships with all four bricks: Kindness, Trust, Celebration, and Real Apologies.
I use my INNER GPS — my own values, my own sense of right — when the pressure to go along is loudest.
I say something when something is wrong. One sentence. Said normally. That is enough.
I protect my memory, my feelings, my personal space, and my online life.
I know the difference between a happy secret and a heavy one.
I forgive what I am ready to forgive — for my own sake, not for theirs.
I give kindness without the receipt.
And when I need help — when something is bigger than my Power-Ups can handle — I ask for it. Knowing when to call for backup is the most advanced skill in the book.
I am not perfect. I will get confused, make mistakes, and sometimes forget the right Power-Up. That is okay.
I have the map. I have the tools. I trust myself to keep growing.
I am a Playground Protector.
I am a Playground Protector's trusted grown-up.
I read this book. I had the conversations. I know the vocabulary.
I will use it — not just tell them to use it.
I will share my own stories with the tricks in this book, because my honesty makes theirs possible.
I will ask "which Power-Up would you use?" when something hard is happening.
I will celebrate their bravery when I see it — especially the small moves.
I will be the person they call when something is too big for their Power-Ups alone.
## Resources
If something in this book raised a concern that needs more than Power-Ups — here is where to start.
Talk to your child's school counselor. Ask specifically what the school's process is.
Stomp Out Bullying: stompoutbullying.org
Pacer's National Bullying Prevention Center: pacer.org/bullying
Common Sense Media: commonsensemedia.org — age guides for every platform.
Internet Matters: internetmatters.org — guides by age and issue.
National Domestic Violence Hotline: thehotline.org or 1-800-799-7233
Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline: 1-800-422-4453
Your child's pediatrician can refer you to a child psychologist or therapist.
Child Mind Institute: childmind.org — free resources on children's mental health.
Psychology Today therapist finder: psychologytoday.com/us/therapists
The best thing you can do after reading this book is keep talking. Use the shared vocabulary. Ask the questions from the Level Up Together sections. Share your own stories. The book gave you the start. The relationship gives you the rest.
You have the map. You have the tools.
You’re a Playground Protector.
## How to get the most out of this book
A few small things make a big difference. You don't have to do all of them — pick what fits your kid.
- 📖 Read it together, not at them. The Tricky Players land best as a shared story. Let your child react, argue, and decide who reminds them of someone.
- ⚡ Use the Power-Up question. When something hard happens in real life, ask “which Power-Up would you use here?” It turns a lecture into a game they already know the rules to.
- 🗣️ Share your own stories. Tell them about a tricky person you met. Your honesty is what makes theirs possible.
- 🚦 Watch the Traffic Light sections. Those mark the moments that are bigger than Power-Ups — where the right move is to get a trusted grown-up. Make sure they know you're that grown-up.
- 💛 Don't let the labels become weapons. The goal is recognizing behavior, never name-calling a sibling or classmate. “That felt like a Whisper Game” — not “you're a Bryant.”
- 🎉 Celebrate the small brave moves. One honest sentence, said calmly, is a win. Notice it out loud.
Shae Stovell is a writer and craftsperson and the creator behind Noble Father Creations . He has spent years studying how people influence, pressure, and manipulate each other — and how ordinary, kind people can learn to see it coming.
Playground Protectors is where that work meets the person who matters most to him: his daughter. It takes the hardest-won lessons about tricky behavior and hands them to kids in a language they actually enjoy — missions, heroes, and Power-Ups instead of warnings and worry.
His hope is simple: that the children who read this grow up a little harder to trick, a little quicker to trust themselves, and a lot quicker to ask for help when they need it.
