### day

**name:** Martin

**when:** A Tuesday in the winter retreat

**where:** A dharma centre in the French Alps


**para**

- Ngöndro at six. He has completed 400,000 prostrations in his life and he can tell you what that did to his knees and also what it did to something else that he has no vocabulary for outside this room.
- He is fifty-four. He sold a flat in Lyon in 2009 to move here. His pension is what it is. He is not resentful about this — he wants that understood — he made a choice and he would defend it at a dinner party.
- At ten the centre director asks him to take on the accounts for the new retreat building, because he was an accountant. He says yes. He is given a folder. In the folder are transfers he does not understand to an entity he has not heard of, and he sits with the folder for a long time, and then he closes it and takes it back and says he doesn't think he has the time after all.
- At lunch a woman named Ilse, who has been here longer than he has, mentions a student who left in 2016. She uses the phrase *broke samaya* and then changes the subject, and Martin, who has taken the same vows, feels the temperature drop about two degrees.
- He took empowerment from the lama in 2011. He remembers the joy of it. He also remembers, and has never told anyone he remembers, that the explanation of what the vow forbade came after the vow, not before.
- At night he lies in a small cold room and thinks about a report that was published a few years ago about a different centre and a different teacher, and about the fact that the organization commissioned it itself, and about the sentence in it that used the word samaya. And then he does what he always does with that thought, which is to recognize it as an obscuration and to bring the mind back to the breath. It works. That is the part he cannot get past: it works.



## Sikhism
*Dharmic*


### Opening

Your Gurus took the office of religious middleman and abolished it. The tenth handed authority to a book so that no living man could ever claim it again. That is one of the most deliberate anti-control acts in religious history — which makes it worth asking why so much control still operates in Punjab and in the diaspora under Sikh cover, and who is running it.


### Overview

~25–30 million Sikhs, homeland in Punjab with a major global diaspora; founded on devotion to one God, equality, honest work, and service; scripture itself (Guru Granth Sahib) is the eternal Guru.


### Origin

Founded by Guru Nanak (15th–16th c. Punjab); ten human Gurus; martial consolidation under persecution; the Khalsa (1699); scriptural guruship ended human succession — a deliberate anti-clerical design.


### authority

- No priesthood by design; in practice: gurdwara management committees, the SGPC (statutory body managing historic gurdwaras), jathedars of the takhts, and deras (sect-like guru movements around living masters — doctrinally contested).
- Committee politics and SGPC elections entangle religious authority with party politics. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### money

- Golak (donation box) revenues of major gurdwaras are substantial; langar economies; diaspora remittances; dera empires around living gurus (Dera Sacha Sauda's convicted leader controlled a corporate-scale operation). [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### exit

- Amritdhari lapse carries community standing costs; family honor economies police marriage and appearance; leaving a dera can mean losing an entire service-and-employment ecosystem.


### whoBenefits

- Gurdwara committee power-holders and the parties that capture them; dera chiefs converting devotion into vote banks courted by politicians; family patriarchy borrowing religious sanction. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### healthy

- The tradition's built-in defenses: no priests, congregational scripture access, langar's radical equality; diaspora gurdwaras with elected transparent boards; Sikh institutions confronting dera abuses.


### timeline

- 1469–1539 — Guru Nanak's ministry in Punjab; rejection of caste, priestcraft, and ritual monopoly — Founded explicitly as a critique of religious hierarchy — anti-control by design.
- 1539–1604 — Successor Gurus; Amritsar founded; Adi Granth compiled 1604 — Scripture is standardized early, reducing interpretive monopoly.
- 1606–1675 — Martyrdoms of Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur under Mughal rule — Persecution forges a martial, self-defending community.
- 1699 — Guru Gobind Singh creates the Khalsa — Collective identity with visible markers and a shared code.
- 1708 — Guruship passes to the scripture (Guru Granth Sahib), ending human succession — A deliberate structural safeguard against personality cults — the tradition's core anti-guru move.
- 1799–1849 — Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh; then British annexation — Statehood and its loss; institutions reorganize under colonial law.
- 1873–1925 — Singh Sabha reform; Gurdwara Act creates the SGPC — Control of historic gurdwaras becomes a statutory, electable prize — religion enters party politics. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1947 — Partition devastates Punjab; mass displacement — Community trauma and diaspora formation.
- 1984 — Operation Blue Star; assassination of Indira Gandhi; anti-Sikh massacres — State violence against the community's holiest site; unresolved justice shapes politics to this day. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- 1990s–present — Global diaspora growth; dera movements expand; Dera Sacha Sauda leader convicted 2017 — Living-guru movements — the very thing scriptural guruship was meant to prevent — become major power centers. [COURT RECORD]


### demographics

**adherents:** ~25–30 million. [ACADEMIC SOURCE: Pew, Indian census]

**regions:** Punjab, India (majority); significant diaspora in Canada, UK, US, Australia, Malaysia, East Africa, Italy.

**branches:** Mainstream Khalsa Sikhism; Nihang, Namdhari, Nirankari and other sects; numerous deras (some accepted, some doctrinally rejected as heterodox).

**trend:** Growing in the diaspora; declining observance of visible markers among some diaspora youth; dera membership substantial among marginalized-caste Punjabis, a fact usually left out of official accounts. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**participation:** Gurdwara attendance is high relative to many traditions, but institutional authority is weak by design — there is no clergy that can excommunicate an individual.


### info

- Committee and SGPC politics determine which preachers get platforms; excommunication (chhaikka) of dissenting scholars has been used against academics whose historical work displeased authorities. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Dera movements exercise strong internal information control around their living gurus, resembling the guru-obedience patterns the tradition formally rejects. [COURT RECORD / FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]
- Community honor pressure suppresses public discussion of caste within Sikhism (separate gurdwaras by caste exist despite doctrine), and of abuse. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### children

- Naam karan naming and Amrit initiation are meant to be chosen — initiation is voluntary and typically adolescent or adult, a genuine structural safeguard.
- Uncut hair and turban for boys begins in early childhood, so visible identity is assigned before consent and carries school-bullying and workplace costs later. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Punjabi schools and camps build identity; family honor expectations around marriage and appearance begin young, particularly for girls.


### gender

- Doctrine is explicitly egalitarian — women may lead prayers and perform all religious functions; the gap between that doctrine and practice is the story here.
- Women are excluded in practice from many senior committee and kirtan roles at major historic gurdwaras. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Female-selective abortion produced severely skewed sex ratios in Punjab despite clear doctrinal condemnation — one of the sharpest doctrine/practice gaps in this codex. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Dowry and caste-endogamous marriage persist against explicit teaching; honor pressure on daughters' marriage choices is well documented.
- Dera guru sexual abuse convictions demonstrate the danger of the living-guru model. [COURT RECORD]


### moneyTable

- Golak (donation box) offerings — Gurdwara operations and langar — Very large cash flows at historic gurdwaras with contested oversight; committee elections fought over control — Committees, SGPC, and genuinely the langar hall [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Langar and seva — Free food and voluntary service — Genuinely one of the least coercive religious institutions in this codex — the risk is only in labor expectation and honor pressure — The public, and the community's reputation
- Diaspora remittances and building funds — Gurdwara construction — Factional control fights over management and, occasionally, litigation and violence over committees — Committee factions [COURT RECORD: diaspora gurdwara disputes]
- Dera economies — Support the living guru's mission — Corporate-scale operations with total internal authority and political protection — Dera leadership and their families [COURT RECORD]


### exitTable

- Formal religious penalty — Rare — No clergy can excommunicate an ordinary member; chhaikka is used mainly against public figures — Accurately: there is little formal exit penalty.
- Family and honor — Yes — Cutting hair, removing turban, marrying outside caste or faith triggers family rupture — “That's Punjabi culture, not Sikhi.”
- Community standing — Moderate — Gurdwara social networks, marriage prospects, and business trust in tight diaspora communities — “Everyone is welcome in a gurdwara.”
- Dera exit — Yes — Loss of an entire service, housing, and employment ecosystem; labeled traitor to the guru — “Following a saint is voluntary.”


### whoPays

- Girls and women, through dowry, sex-selective abortion, and honor pressure that doctrine explicitly forbids.
- Dalit Sikhs, facing caste exclusion including separate gurdwaras.
- Dera followers subjected to documented abuse.
- Youth who cut their hair, bearing family rupture over a visible marker assigned in infancy.
- Scholars excommunicated for historical research. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Medium — Scripture and the Rehat Maryada are published, and they mostly forbid the coercion that occurs.
- Informal enforcement — High — Honor, marriage networks, and community reputation carry nearly everything.
- Leadership distance — High — No clergy to hold responsible; committees disclaim family and cultural conduct.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Low — Unusually clear doctrine — which makes the practice gap harder to defend, not easier.
- Cultural outsourcing — Very high — Caste, dowry, and sex selection are all attributed to Punjabi culture rather than Sikhism — a defense that is partly true and wholly convenient.
- Volunteer enforcement — High — Relatives and community members enforce appearance and marriage norms.
- Sacred secrecy — Low — Congregational openness and public scripture reading limit secrecy — a genuine structural strength.
- Exit cost denial — Medium — 'No one is forced' is largely true institutionally and much less true within families.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Living-guru (dera) movements

**origin:** Post-1708, various figures claimed continuing personal guruship despite the scriptural succession; the modern dera phenomenon expanded through the 20th century. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** None within Sikh doctrine — this is the precise thing the scriptural guruship was created to prevent. Their appeal is real, though: deras have served marginalized-caste Punjabis whom mainstream gurdwaras treated poorly.

**expired:** It was never legitimate doctrinally, and the outcomes are documented: the leader of one of the largest deras was convicted of rape and of conspiracy to murder. [COURT RECORD]

**benefitsNow:** Dera chiefs and their families, running large operations with political protection because their followers vote in blocs.

**mechanism:** Committee and SGPC control of gurdwaras

**origin:** The 1925 Gurdwara Act made control of historic gurdwaras a statutory, electable prize. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** A genuine reform: it wrested shrines from hereditary custodians who had been treating them as private property.

**expired:** It converted religious authority into an electoral asset. Committee control means control of very large cash flows and of who is allowed to preach, and party politics followed the money in.

**benefitsNow:** Political parties and committee factions. Scholars have been excommunicated for historical research that displeased them. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]

**mechanism:** Caste practice inside a tradition that abolished it

**origin:** Punjabi caste structures that persisted through Sikhism's explicit doctrinal rejection of them. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Nothing Sikh. Guru Nanak attacked caste directly, and langar exists specifically to break it.

**expired:** It has no doctrinal defense at all, which is why it is always defended as culture. Separate caste-based gurdwaras exist, and inter-caste marriage still triggers family rupture.

**benefitsNow:** Established landowning families and marriage networks. Note that the deniability here is total precisely because doctrine is on your side and practice is not.

**mechanism:** Honor pressure on daughters

**origin:** Punjabi honor codes surviving alongside a scripture that declares women equal. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Kin-group status management, not religion.

**expired:** Punjab's sex ratio became one of the most skewed in India despite unambiguous doctrinal condemnation of female infanticide. The gap between what your scripture says and what your community does is the widest in this codex.

**benefitsNow:** Family reputation economies, and the men whose standing depends on their daughters' compliance.

### leverage

- Dera leaders deliver bloc votes and receive political protection in exchange; convictions arrived only after evidence became unbearable. Devotion converted into electoral currency. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Control of historic gurdwaras means control of very large donation flows, making religious office a party-political prize with real money attached. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Diaspora gurdwara factions have litigated and occasionally fought over committee control — remittances from abroad are the asset being contested. [COURT RECORD]


### hardQuestions

- Guru Gobind Singh ended human guruship. Explain how a living dera guru is anything other than the thing he abolished.
- Your scripture rejects caste. Ask why your family will not accept the marriage, and ask them to cite a line.
- Ask your gurdwara committee for the golak accounts. Note whether the answer is a number or an insult.
- Female infanticide is condemned outright in your tradition. Ask why Punjab's sex ratio says what it says, and who was silent.
- A dera leader was convicted of rape. Name a Sikh political figure who returned his support and said why.
- You were taught these are cultural matters, not religious ones. Ask why culture always wins when it conflicts with your Gurus.


### closing

- You have the strongest structural position of any reader of this codex. No priest can absolve you, no clergy can expel you, your scripture is in your hands and read aloud in public, and langar seats everyone on the same floor by design. The machinery in your community is not built into your religion — it was smuggled in alongside it.
- Which means your work is not deconstruction. It is enforcement. Every abuse in this profile is already illegal under your own doctrine. You do not need a new belief; you need to hold your community to the one it already claims.

### day

**name:** Jasleen

**when:** A Tuesday in Vaisakh

**where:** Southall, west London


**para**

- Her father does Nitnem at five and the sound of it through the wall is the sound of her entire childhood. She is twenty-four and she can hear him from her old bedroom and she is glad she came home for the week.
- At the gurdwara at seven for the langar shift, because her mother volunteers Tuesdays and Jasleen is filling in. Two hundred people will eat here today, anyone at all, no questions, on the same floor. She has thought many times that whatever else her community has got wrong, it got this profoundly right.
- In the kitchen the aunties are discussing the committee election. There is money in it — the golak, the hall hire, the building fund — and there are two factions, and one of them took the other to court in 2019. Jasleen listens and does not participate. Nobody publishes accounts. Nobody has ever published accounts.
- At eleven her cousin Simran calls, crying, because Simran's parents have found out about her boyfriend, whose family is Ravidasia. Jasleen says all the right things. She does not say the thing she is actually thinking, which is that the Guru Granth Sahib is extremely clear about this and that everyone in both houses can read it, and that it will make no difference whatsoever.
- In the afternoon someone mentions a dera leader, and a conviction, and a journalist who was shot, and a man at the next table says that it was all politics. Nobody argues with him. Jasleen thinks about how there is a photograph of that dera leader in her great-uncle's shop in Jalandhar.
- At night her father asks, not unkindly, whether she is thinking about keeping her hair long again. She cut it at nineteen. She says she doesn't know. He says the Guru gave it as a gift. She says she knows. And she does know, and she also knows that he means it about the gift and not about the neighbours, and that his brother does not, and that she has never been able to explain why that difference matters so much to her.



## Jainism
*Dharmic*


### Opening

Your tradition took nonviolence further than anyone. It also built a small, brilliant, tightly woven world in which everyone knows everything — and that visibility, not any priest, is what does the enforcing. There is no one to disobey here. That is precisely why it is hard to see.


### Overview

~4–5 million adherents, mostly in India; an ancient path of radical nonviolence (ahimsa), asceticism, and non-absolutism, with an influential lay merchant community.


### Origin

Contemporary with early Buddhism; Mahavira (5th c. BCE) as the last of 24 tirthankaras; monastic-lay symbiosis: ascetics depend entirely on laity, laity earn merit by supporting ascetics.


### authority

- Monastic orders (Svetambara/Digambara lineages) with acharyas; lay temple trusts and caste-community councils; family and community honor systems.
- Authority is soft but total within community bounds: reputation, marriage networks, and business webs enforce conformity without any formal police. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### money

- Temple trusts with significant wealth; ritual sponsorships auctioned (bidding for rites); community levies; the diamond/trading-community overlap makes religious and business networks one fabric.
- Public austerity events generate family status — honor economics as the currency. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### exit

- Leaving costs marriage networks and business trust simultaneously — the community's commercial integration is the enforcement mechanism.
- Sallekhana (end-of-life fasting) sits in genuine ethical contest between voluntary religious dying and family-honor pressure; Indian courts have litigated it. [COURT RECORD: Rajasthan HC 2015, stayed by Supreme Court]


### whoBenefits

- Trust boards and community elites controlling ritual honors and match networks; families accruing status from members' austerities.


### healthy

- Anekantavada (many-sidedness) as a native anti-dogmatism resource; transparent trusts; the community's genuine philanthropy and low-violence ethic.


### timeline

- c. 9th–5th c. BCE — Tradition of 24 tirthankaras; Parshvanatha and then Mahavira (c. 599–527 BCE) — Radical nonviolence and asceticism established as a full path outside Vedic priesthood.
- c. 300 BCE–100 CE — Svetambara/Digambara division; Agamas compiled — Institutional split over monastic practice, especially clothing and women's capacity for liberation.
- 100–1200 CE — Royal patronage in western and southern India; temple building; monastic orders formalize — Wealthy lay patronage creates a durable temple economy.
- 1200–1800 — Muslim and then Maratha-era adaptation; merchant communities consolidate — The community's commercial specialization becomes its social infrastructure.
- 1800s — Colonial-era reform; print culture; diaspora trading networks — Community identity codified; institutions modernize.
- 1900s — Global diaspora (East Africa, UK, US); institutional philanthropy expands — Diaspora wealth funds temples and community institutions internationally.
- 1970s–present — Diaspora temple building; animal-welfare and vegetarian advocacy — Ethical influence far larger than the community's size.
- 2015 — Rajasthan High Court rules santhara (sallekhana) illegal; Supreme Court stays the ruling — The state and the tradition collide over religious dying and family pressure. [COURT RECORD]
- 2000s–present — Debates over women's monastic status, caste practice, and business-community insularity — Internal reform pressure in a small, tightly networked community.


### demographics

**adherents:** ~4–5 million, overwhelmingly in India. [ACADEMIC SOURCE: Indian census]

**regions:** Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh; diaspora in the UK, US, Kenya, Belgium (Antwerp diamond trade), Canada.

**branches:** Svetambara (further divided into Murtipujaka, Sthanakvasi, Terapanth) and Digambara; numerous monastic lineages.

**trend:** Small and roughly stable, with very low fertility, high education, and high urbanization; India's most literate and among its wealthiest religious communities. [GOVERNMENT REPORT: census data]

**participation:** Unusually high correlation between identity and practice; the community's small size and commercial integration mean social visibility is total — everyone is known.


### info

- Information control is minimal doctrinally — anekantavada (many-sidedness) is an explicit epistemic humility principle, one of the strongest native anti-dogmatism resources in this codex.
- Practical control runs through reputation instead: what the community knows about a family circulates instantly through business and marriage networks. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Monastic authority over lay questions can discourage dissent on practices such as extreme fasting. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### children

- Dietary restriction from birth (no root vegetables in strict practice, no eating after dark in some households) makes the child's body a site of religious identity from infancy.
- Child fasting during festivals (Paryushan) earns family status; the honor incentive can push children past healthy limits. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Child renunciation (bal diksha) — minors taking monastic vows — has been publicly criticized and litigated in India as a consent problem. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### gender

- Digambara tradition historically holds that women cannot attain liberation in a female body; Svetambara disagrees — a doctrinal gender asymmetry stated in the sources. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Nuns outnumber monks in several orders yet remain subordinate in authority and ritual precedence.
- Menstrual exclusion from temple and ritual participation is common practice.
- Marriage within community and caste is strongly expected; dowry persists despite the ethic of non-possession. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### moneyTable

- Temple trusts and construction donations — Temple building and upkeep — Large trusts with concentrated board control; donor prestige hierarchies — Trust boards, prominent donor families
- Auctioned ritual honors (bidding for rites) — Support the temple through devotion — Explicit purchase of religious status — wealth converted directly into sanctity — Temples, and the status of winning families
- Monastic support and event sponsorship — Sustain ascetics — Sponsorship is public and ranked; status pressure on families of modest means — Monastic orders, sponsoring families' reputations
- Community business networks and credit — Mutual commercial trust — Religious standing and creditworthiness become the same thing — dissent is economically expensive — Established merchant families [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### exitTable

- Marriage and business networks — Yes — Community integration means religious standing and commercial trust are one system — “Business is business.”
- Family honor — Yes — Public austerity and dietary conformity are family status; deviation is visible immediately — “No one forces anyone to fast.”
- Formal religious sanction — Rare — No excommunication apparatus for ordinary members — Accurately: institutional exit penalties are low.
- Spiritual framing — Yes — Karmic consequence for harm and laxity; guilt as the primary enforcement — “That is simply what karma means.”


### whoPays

- Women, under liberation-capacity doctrine, ritual exclusion, and dowry practice.
- Children pushed into competitive fasting or minor renunciation.
- Elderly people in contested santhara cases where family honor may shade voluntary dying.
- Families of modest means, competing in a visible sponsorship economy.
- Anyone whose independence would cost them the credit and marriage network at once.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Medium — Monastic codes and temple rules are written; social enforcement is not.
- Informal enforcement — Very high — Reputation within a small, dense community is the entire mechanism.
- Leadership distance — High — Monastic orders disclaim lay conduct; trusts disclaim family behavior.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Medium — Anekantavada cuts both ways: genuine humility, and a ready answer that any practice is just one view.
- Cultural outsourcing — High — Dowry and caste practice attributed to Indian culture despite non-possession ethics.
- Volunteer enforcement — Very high — Families and neighbors enforce; no institution issues instructions.
- Sacred secrecy — Low — Practice is highly public — visibility is the enforcement, not secrecy.
- Exit cost denial — High — 'Nothing is compulsory in Jainism' — said within a community where everything is observed.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Purity ranking through austerity

**origin:** Ancient ascetic practice in which renunciation genuinely was the path, undertaken by monastics who had left everything. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Voluntary, radical, and total — for people who had already given up family, property, and status. It ranked no one because everyone practicing had exited the status economy entirely.

**expired:** Transplanted into lay life with public visibility, austerity became a competitive display. Families accrue status from a child's fast. That inverts the original meaning completely: renunciation now buys the very status it was meant to abandon.

**benefitsNow:** Family reputation, and community elites who set the standard. The cost falls on children pushed past their limits and families of modest means who cannot compete.

**mechanism:** Auctioned ritual honors

**origin:** Temple funding practice in which the right to perform certain rites is bid for. [PATTERN OBSERVED]

**thenPurpose:** A transparent way to fund temple upkeep from a prosperous merchant community.

**expired:** It is the most literal transaction in this codex: wealth converted directly into sanctity, in public, with a price. Non-possession is the tradition's central ethic, and the ritual economy ranks people by possession.

**benefitsNow:** Temple trusts, and the status of the families that win. A community founded on non-attachment now auctions proximity to the sacred.

**mechanism:** Digambara doctrine that women cannot attain liberation

**origin:** Classical sectarian dispute; Svetambara texts disagree. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Argued from claims about the female body and nudity requirements for final renunciation.

**expired:** The Svetambara position proves the doctrine is contested, not necessary. A metaphysical ceiling on half the population, defended by anatomy, in a tradition whose nuns outnumber its monks.

**benefitsNow:** Male monastic precedence and authority. Nothing else.

**mechanism:** Child renunciation (bal diksha)

**origin:** Long-standing practice of youthful monastic entry. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Early entry into a lifelong discipline in a world where adult life choices were made young anyway.

**expired:** A minor cannot meaningfully consent to permanent renunciation of family, property, education, and sexuality. Indian courts and public criticism have raised exactly this, and family honor is an obvious confounding motive. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]

**benefitsNow:** Monastic orders gaining lifetime members, and families gaining prestige from a child's renunciation.

### leverage

- Community integration means religious standing and commercial credit are the same asset — dissent is expensive in a currency that has nothing to do with belief. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Temple trusts hold substantial wealth under concentrated board control, with donor prestige hierarchies determining influence. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- The community's genuine philanthropy and animal-welfare influence far exceeds its size — worth stating plainly, because it is the truest thing on this page. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### hardQuestions

- Non-possession is your central ethic. Explain the auction for ritual honors.
- If a child's fast brings the family status, ask honestly whose fast it is.
- The Svetambara tradition says women can attain liberation. Ask a Digambara authority why his position, which excludes half of humanity, should be the one that stands.
- A minor cannot sign a contract. Explain how a minor can renounce the world permanently.
- Ask your temple trust for accounts. Note whether the request is answered or absorbed.
- Nobody here forces anything — that is your community's most accurate claim and its most complete defense. Ask why total visibility makes force unnecessary.


### closing

- Anekantavada — the doctrine that reality has many sides and no single view captures it — is the single best anti-dogmatism principle any religion produced. It belongs to you. Use it on your own community's certainties, not only on outsiders'.
- Your ethic of nonviolence is not diminished by asking who benefits from a child's hunger or a widow's silence. It is completed by it. Ahimsa that stops at the community's reputation was never ahimsa; it was etiquette.

### day

**name:** Nita

**when:** A Tuesday during Paryushan

**where:** Ahmedabad


**para**

- Day five of the fast. She has done this since she was fourteen. Her body is quiet and her mind is unusually clear and there is something in it that is genuinely not about anyone watching, and she wants that noted.
- Her daughter Aarti is nine and is on day two. Aarti wants to reach four days because Priya from the building reached four days last year and there was an announcement at the temple. Nita has told her that four is not necessary. Aarti has heard that four is available.
- At ten the auction. The right to perform tomorrow's rite goes for a figure that is read aloud, and the family that wins is applauded, and everyone in the hall now knows what everyone in the hall can afford. Nita's husband bid twice and stopped. She watched his face when he stopped.
- At lunch — which she does not eat — her sister-in-law mentions that the Mehtas' son is not fasting at all this year, and that people have noticed, and that it is a shame because the girl they were considering for him is from a very observant family. Nothing further is said. Nothing further needs to be.
- In the afternoon a supplier calls her husband about credit. The supplier is from the community. The conversation is friendly and it is also, Nita understands completely, a conversation about their standing at the temple. These are the same conversation. They have always been the same conversation.
- At nine Aarti asks if she can stop, and then, immediately, asks whether Nita will be disappointed. Nita says of course not, sweetheart. And then she hears herself add — lightly, almost as a joke — *but you were so close.* And she lies awake later, hungry and clear-minded and completely awake, thinking about the four words she added and about who exactly they were for.



## Taoism / Daoism
*East Asian*


### Opening

You may have come to this through breath, movement, or a book that told you to stop striving — and found something true. But this is also the tradition where almost nothing is written down, no one can be verified, and 'you are resisting the flow' can be said to you by a man charging four thousand dollars for the next level. Softness is not the same as safety.


### Overview

Chinese religious-philosophical tradition of alignment with the Dao; ranges from philosophical texts (Laozi, Zhuangzi) to organized religious lineages, temple networks, ritual masters, and internal-alchemy schools.


### Origin

Classical texts (~4th c. BCE); organized religious Taoism from the Celestial Masters (2nd c. CE); imperial patronage cycles; suppression and state management in the PRC; global diffusion through qigong, tai chi, and wellness culture.


### authority

- Lineage transmission and ritual-master ordination; in the PRC, the state-run Taoist Association licenses clergy and temples — religion under bureaucratic management. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- In the diffuse Western market: self-authorized masters with invented or embellished lineages. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### money

- Temple fees, ritual services (funerals, exorcisms, blessings), fortune-telling and feng shui economies, and the global qigong/wellness course market.
- PRC temple tourism monetization: ticketed sacred sites with revenue flowing through state-adjacent management. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT — verify specifics]


### exit

- Low formal exit costs; the risk zone is master-student capture in small schools where 'transmission' justifies control and fees.


### whoBenefits

- The Chinese state managing religion as heritage-tourism and social control; ritual-service providers; Western lineage entrepreneurs monetizing exotic authority.


### healthy

- The philosophical stream's own skepticism of authority and artifice — Zhuangzi is a standing rebuke to religious pomposity; teachers with transparent lineage claims and posted prices.


### timeline

- c. 4th–3rd c. BCE — Daodejing and Zhuangzi circulate — A philosophy explicitly skeptical of rulers, hierarchy, and moral posturing.
- 142 CE — Celestial Masters movement founded; organized religious Daoism with clergy and dues — Philosophy acquires an institution, a priesthood, and a tax — within four centuries of the texts.
- 300–900 CE — Canon formation; Shangqing and Lingbao traditions; imperial patronage cycles — Court favor determines which lineages flourish.
- 1100–1400 — Quanzhen (Complete Perfection) monasticism; Mongol-era patronage — Monastic Daoism institutionalizes; internal alchemy traditions formalize.
- 1400–1900 — Temple networks, ritual specialists, folk-religion integration — Daoist ritual becomes the practical religion of village life across China.
- 1911–1949 — Republican-era suppression as 'superstition'; temple confiscations — Modernizing states treat the tradition as backwardness.
- 1949–1976 — PRC suppression; Cultural Revolution destroys temples and lineages — Massive rupture of transmission — a real persecution that must be stated alongside any critique.
- 1957 / 1980s — China Taoist Association established; post-Mao revival under state licensing — Clergy and temples operate by government permission. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1980s–2000s — Qigong boom; Falun Gong emerges and is banned in 1999 — Mass practice movements and their suppression — state control of the spiritual field. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- 1990s–present — Global wellness market absorbs qigong, tai chi, feng shui; temple tourism monetized — Western lineage entrepreneurship with no verifiable accountability. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### demographics

**adherents:** Extremely difficult to count: perhaps 8–20 million formally identifying, while hundreds of millions of Chinese people participate in practices of Daoist origin without any affiliation. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** Mainland China, Taiwan (where temple Daoism is vigorous and unregulated by Beijing), Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, global diaspora.

**branches:** Quanzhen and Zhengyi as the principal ordination lineages; countless local temple traditions; a distinct Western philosophical/wellness stream largely detached from either.

**trend:** State-managed revival in the PRC; strong in Taiwan; the global wellness stream growing fastest and least accountably.

**participation:** The gap between practice and identity is the largest of any tradition here — a person may use feng shui, consult a temple, and practice qigong while reporting no religion at all.


### info

- In the PRC, clergy registration, temple licensing, and content restrictions place religious information under state administration. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Lineage secrecy and 'the transmission cannot be explained' claims make credentials unverifiable — the central vulnerability in the Western market. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Energy-diagnosis framing ('your qi is blocked because you resist') makes the teacher the sole interpreter of the student's own body. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### children

- Little formal child initiation in most traditions; children participate in family temple observance and ancestor rites rather than being enrolled.
- Martial-arts and temple training schools for children can be intense, and in some documented commercial schools abusive. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Fortune-telling and horoscope framing applied to children can shape marriage, career, and naming decisions before consent. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### gender

- Female priests and Daoist nuns have a genuine historical presence — comparatively strong among traditions in this codex. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Internal-alchemy literature contains gender-differentiated practice, sometimes framing female bodies as requiring correction.
- The high-risk zone is the modern teacher–student market: sexual-energy and 'dual cultivation' framings have been used to obtain sex from students. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### moneyTable

- Temple offerings, incense, divination, and fortune slips — Blessing, guidance, temple upkeep — Fee-per-answer religion targeting anxiety about health, money, and marriage — Temples, ritual specialists, and in the PRC, state-adjacent management
- Ritual services (funerals, exorcisms, geomancy) — Care for the dead; harmony of place — Priced life-crisis services with no standard rates; escalation during grief — Ritual masters and their networks
- Qigong, tai chi, and internal-alchemy courses — Health and cultivation — Escalating levels, initiation fees, and secret transmissions — a certification pyramid with no external validator — Teachers and lineage entrepreneurs
- Temple tourism and ticketed sacred sites — Heritage preservation — Sacred access converted to admission revenue under management with unclear beneficiaries — Management companies and local government [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT — verify specifics]


### exitTable

- Formal penalty — Very low — No membership, no excommunication, no shunning apparatus — Accurately: institutional Daoism has among the lowest exit costs here.
- Master–student capture — Yes in small schools — Years of fees and deference; leaving framed as losing the transmission or damaging one's qi — “The student simply stopped practicing.”
- Financial loss — Yes — Escalating course and initiation payments with nothing transferable — “They paid for teaching they received.”
- Spiritual framing — Moderate — Misfortune or illness attributed to abandoning practice or offending the master — “That's just how energy works.”


### whoPays

- Students of self-certified Western masters, financially and sometimes sexually exploited.
- Grieving and ill people paying for outcome-promising rituals.
- Falun Gong practitioners and other unregistered groups, under documented state persecution. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Children in commercial martial-arts boarding schools.
- Chinese Daoist clergy, whose religious life requires state permission.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — High deniability — Almost nothing is written down — no membership rules, no published requirements, no receipts.
- Informal enforcement — High — Master's approval and lineage standing are the only currency, and both are undocumented.
- Leadership distance — Very high — No central body of any kind outside state associations.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Very high — 'Flow,' 'balance,' and 'non-action' can rationalize any instruction or any harm.
- Cultural outsourcing — High — Problems attributed to Chinese cultural context or to the student's Western misunderstanding.
- Volunteer enforcement — Medium — Senior students protect the master's reputation and gatekeep access.
- Sacred secrecy — High — Unverifiable secret transmission is the core structural weakness.
- Exit cost denial — Medium — Institutionally accurate; individually false inside a capture relationship.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Unverifiable lineage transmission

**origin:** Oral and initiatory transmission in Chinese religious Daoism, with secrecy protecting genuinely difficult and sometimes dangerous practices. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** In a lineage community, everyone knew who trained whom. Secrecy from outsiders coexisted with total transparency inside.

**expired:** In the global market there is no inside. A Western teacher can claim any lineage and no one can check, because checking is framed as disrespect and the records were destroyed in the 20th century anyway.

**benefitsNow:** Anyone willing to claim credentials they do not have. This is the structural vulnerability that defines the modern tradition.

**mechanism:** 'You are resisting' — flow language as compliance tool

**origin:** Classical wu wei: effortless action, non-forcing, alignment with the Dao. Philosophically serious and originally anti-authoritarian. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Zhuangzi used these ideas to mock rulers, moralists, and religious pomposity. The concept was a weapon against control.

**expired:** Inverted entirely. A command phrased as 'stop resisting the flow' is still a command, and it now arrives from the person selling the flow. The most anti-authoritarian vocabulary in Chinese thought became a script for teacher authority.

**benefitsNow:** Teachers whose instructions cannot be refused without the refusal itself becoming evidence of the student's blockage.

**mechanism:** Energy diagnosis as sole interpretive authority

**origin:** Traditional Chinese medical and internal-alchemy frameworks describing qi. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** A working physiology in a pre-modern medical system, applied by practitioners embedded in accountable communities.

**expired:** When only the master can read your qi, only the master can say whether you are improving, and only the master can say what the next payment buys. Your own body is no longer evidence you can access.

**benefitsNow:** The diagnosing teacher, who occupies the position of both physician and salesman with no licensing body in between.

**mechanism:** State licensing of clergy and temples (PRC)

**origin:** The China Taoist Association (1957) and post-1980s revival under government registration. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Framed as restoring a tradition the state itself had devastated.

**expired:** Restoration under permission is management. Clergy are licensed, content is restricted, and sacred sites are ticketed heritage attractions with revenue flowing through state-adjacent administration.

**benefitsNow:** The state, which converts a suppressed religion into managed heritage and tourism income.

### leverage

- The Chinese state manages Daoism as licensed heritage: clergy registered, temples ticketed, and sacred sites operated as tourism assets under state-adjacent administration. [OFFICIAL POLICY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- The global wellness market monetizes qigong, tai chi, and feng shui through certification pyramids in which the upstream certifier profits from every practitioner they license. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Ritual services priced during illness and bereavement extract most from people least able to evaluate the claim. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### hardQuestions

- Ask your teacher for his lineage: names, dates, and a person alive who can confirm it. Note whether you get an answer or a lesson about your need for certainty.
- Ask for a price list for every level, in writing, in advance. Note what happens.
- If only he can read your qi, ask what evidence would ever tell you he was wrong.
- Zhuangzi mocked authority. Explain how deference to a master is Daoist.
- If a practice requires sexual contact with your teacher, ask him to produce the text — and then ask a scholar whether he read it correctly.
- You were taught that questioning shows rigidity. Ask who benefits from a framework where scepticism is a symptom.


### closing

- Your tradition's founding texts are the least authoritarian documents in this entire codex. Zhuangzi's whole project was deflating people who claimed spiritual authority. Laozi says the sage does not accumulate. Every mechanism on this page is something the source texts would have laughed at.
- So use them the way they were meant to be used. A tradition that says the Dao cannot be captured in words is a poor foundation for anyone claiming to own the words. Keep the practice, keep the philosophy, and stop paying men for access to your own breath.

### day

**name:** Ellen

**para**

- Standing practice at dawn on the deck, forty minutes, and afterwards her hands feel warm and heavy in a way she cannot explain and has stopped trying to. Something happens in her body when she does this. She is not making it up.
- She is sixty-one and retired and has spent, at last count, $18,400 across three years — the foundations course, the intensive, the certification track, two private diagnostics.
- At eleven, the Zoom with Master Wen. Twelve of them in little squares. He looks at her for a moment and says her liver qi is stagnant and that this is why the shoulder has not resolved. She writes it down. She has written down four different explanations for the shoulder across three years and each one has been superseded by the next, and each supersession has cost between four hundred and twelve hundred dollars.
- She asks — and she has been building up to this for two weeks — where the lineage comes from. There is a small pause. He smiles and says that the transmission cannot be put into words, and that her need for a document is the Western mind, and that this is itself something to work on. Three people in the squares nod. Ellen says thank you.
- At lunch she looks up the temple he named. She finds a photograph and a paragraph and nothing that mentions him. She closes the laptop and goes for a walk and tells herself she doesn't need the paperwork, which is a sentence she has said before.
- In the evening her daughter calls from Denver and asks, carefully, how much level three is. Ellen says she hasn't decided. It is $4,800. Her daughter says *mom* and Ellen says *the practice works, Katie* — and it does, that is the thing, the hands go warm and the sleep is better and she is not imagining it. She just cannot explain why the practice working means the man must be paid again.



## Confucianism
*East Asian*


### Opening

There is nothing here to leave. No membership, no baptism, no doctrine you ever agreed to — and that is exactly why this may be the hardest section in the codex to read honestly. You were not recruited. You were raised. And the machinery is your family, which means naming it feels like betrayal before you have even finished the sentence.


### Overview

An ethical-social tradition of self-cultivation, ritual propriety, and relational duty that structured East Asian family, education, and governance for two millennia — religion, philosophy, and social operating system at once.


### Origin

Confucius (551–479 BCE) and successors; imperial orthodoxy from the Han dynasty; the examination system made Confucian texts the gateway to power for 1,300 years; modern revivals serve both cultural renewal and state ideology.


### authority

- No church: authority lives in the family hierarchy, elder–junior relations, teacher–student bonds, and — historically and again today — the state claiming Confucian legitimacy.
- The PRC's promotion of Confucian harmony and filial values doubles as a compliance vocabulary. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### money

- Not donation-based; the extraction is labor, deference, and life-choice control within families — eldercare obligations, career and marriage direction, gendered sacrifice. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Ancestor-rite economies and lineage-hall funds in some regions.


### exit

- There is no membership to resign — which is the trap: one can only be a bad child, a bad student, a disharmonious element. Dissent has no legitimate category.
- Real costs: inheritance, family standing, and in state-Confucian framing, political suspicion.


### whoBenefits

- Senior generations and patriarchs collecting structurally guaranteed deference; states renting the harmony vocabulary to delegitimize dissent; employers importing filial duty into workplace obedience. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### healthy

- The tradition's own corrective: Mencius' right of remonstrance — the duty to correct erring superiors; reciprocity read in both directions; Confucian feminists and reformers reclaiming the ethics from the hierarchy.


### timeline

- 551–479 BCE — Confucius teaches in the state of Lu — An ethic of reciprocal duty — including a superior's duty to be worthy of obedience.
- 4th–3rd c. BCE — Mencius and Xunzi develop rival readings — Mencius asserts the right to remonstrate and even to depose an unworthy ruler — the tradition's own anti-authoritarian resource.
- 136 BCE — Han dynasty establishes Confucian classics as state orthodoxy — An ethic becomes a licensing exam for political power.
- 605–1905 CE — Imperial examination system — For 1,300 years, memorizing a canon is the only route to status — the most durable ideological monopoly in history.
- 960–1279 — Neo-Confucian synthesis (Zhu Xi); lineage halls and clan rules formalize — Family hierarchy is codified as cosmic order; ancestor ritual becomes household law.
- 1300–1900 — Spread to Korea, Japan, Vietnam; widow chastity cults; footbinding culturally entrenched — Gender control intensifies far beyond anything in the founding texts. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1905–1919 — Exams abolished; New Culture Movement attacks Confucianism as feudal — Modernizers identify filial hierarchy as the machinery of oppression.
- 1949–1976 — PRC campaigns against Confucianism, peaking in the Cultural Revolution — A tradition of deference is itself violently suppressed.
- 1980s–2000s — 'Asian values' discourse; Confucius Institutes founded 2004 — Filial and harmony language redeployed for state legitimacy and soft power. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 2010s–present — Official promotion of filial piety and 'harmonious society'; elder-care law — Duty toward parents becomes enforceable state policy. [OFFICIAL POLICY: PRC elderly rights law]


### demographics

**adherents:** Essentially uncountable as a religion: perhaps 6–8 million formal identifiers, while Confucian norms shape family and social life for well over a billion people across East Asia. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** China, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Singapore, and their diasporas.

**branches:** Classical, Neo-Confucian (Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming schools), Korean Seongnihak, Japanese and Vietnamese adaptations, contemporary 'New Confucianism.'

**trend:** Formal religious identification is negligible and stable; cultural and state-sponsored influence is rising in China. Urbanization and low fertility are eroding the multigenerational household the ethic assumes.

**participation:** There is no membership to hold. This entry documents a control grammar embedded in families, schools, and workplaces — which is exactly why it is the hardest pattern in this codex to refuse.


### info

- Historically, the canon was the curriculum, and the curriculum was the only path to advancement — total alignment of knowledge with career. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Contemporary state deployment pairs harmony language with censorship: dissent is framed as disorder rather than as disagreement. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Within families, 'do not shame us' functions as an information rule — problems including abuse must not leave the household. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### children

- Filial obligation attaches at birth and never terminates; obedience is the child's defining virtue in the popular reading.
- Academic pressure operates as religious duty: a child's exam result is family honor, with documented consequences for adolescent mental health. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Career, marriage partner, and residence choices are commonly treated as family decisions rather than individual ones. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Corporal punishment normalized as discipline; 'I did this for you' converts childhood investment into lifelong debt.


### gender

- The Three Obediences and Four Virtues subordinated women to father, husband, and son in the classical formulation. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

- Informal enforcement — Very high — Shame, face, and duty are the entire enforcement apparatus.
- Leadership distance — Total — There is no leadership at all to hold accountable — the purest case of ownerless control in this codex.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — High — Reciprocal duty is the textual reading; one-directional obedience is the practiced one, and defenders can always cite the former.
- Cultural outsourcing — Total — This is the tradition that *is* the culture — the deflection is structurally unanswerable.
- Volunteer enforcement — Total — Parents, aunts, teachers, and employers enforce; no one was ever instructed to.
- Sacred secrecy — Medium — Family privacy norms suppress disclosure of harm.
- Exit cost denial — Very high — 'It's just respect for your parents' — said to someone with no legitimate way to say no.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Filial obedience as unlimited obligation

**origin:** Classical texts describe reciprocal duty; Neo-Confucian codification (Zhu Xi and after) hardened it into hierarchy, and imperial states promoted the one-directional reading. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** In an agrarian society with no pensions, no insurance, and no state welfare, the multigenerational household *was* the safety net. Filial duty was retirement policy.

**expired:** There are now pensions, insurance, and healthcare systems. But the obligation remained and expanded, and in China it became statutory — adult children legally liable for parental support. The safety net became a lien.

**benefitsNow:** The senior generation, and the state, which offloads its welfare costs onto adult children while calling it virtue. Mencius asserted the duty to remonstrate with an erring superior — that half of the ethic simply vanished, and its disappearance was not accidental.

**mechanism:** Face and shame as enforcement

**origin:** Ritual propriety (li) as the ordering of social relations. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** In dense village communities, reputation was the only enforcement available and it applied to everyone including elders.

**expired:** It now runs in one direction. A parent's conduct is not subject to the family's shame; a child's is. And 'do not bring shame on us' functions as an information rule that keeps abuse, debt, illness, and violence inside the house.

**benefitsNow:** Whoever is senior in any given room. And abusers, who are protected by the same rule that protects the family's name.

**mechanism:** Patrilineal ancestor ritual

**origin:** Ancient lineage rites requiring a male descendant to perform offerings. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Continuity of the lineage in a system where property, name, and ritual obligation passed through sons.

**expired:** When ultrasound arrived, a ritual requirement for sons became a demand for the elimination of daughters. Skewed sex ratios across the region are the measurable output of a metaphysical preference. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

**benefitsNow:** Lineage elders and the patrilineal property structure. The cost is paid by daughters who were never born and by the women who were pressured into it.

**mechanism:** Academic achievement as moral duty

**origin:** The imperial examination system (605–1905): thirteen centuries in which memorizing a canon was the sole route to status. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Astonishingly, a meritocratic reform — it opened offices to talent rather than birth in an aristocratic world.

**expired:** The exam is gone; the psychology outlived it by a century. A child's test score is now family honor, and failure is treated as moral defect rather than an outcome. The mental-health consequences are documented. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**benefitsNow:** A tutoring industry of enormous scale, schools competing on rankings, and family status. Not the child.

### leverage

- The Chinese state promotes filial piety and 'harmonious society' as governance vocabulary, converting a family ethic into a compliance frame in which dissent is disorder rather than disagreement. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Elder-support obligations have been written into law, transferring the state's welfare costs to adult children under the language of virtue. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Confucius Institutes and cultural diplomacy export the harmony vocabulary internationally as soft power. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Employers import filial duty into workplace hierarchy: overtime as loyalty, obedience as respect, exhaustion as virtue. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### hardQuestions

- Mencius said a son must remonstrate with an erring father. Ask whoever taught you obedience why they left that part out.
- If duty is reciprocal, name the obligation your parents owe you that they would accept being held to.
- 'Do not shame the family' has kept violence, debt, and abuse inside houses for centuries. Ask who that rule protects, in your specific family.
- If sons are required for ancestor rites, ask what happened to the daughters — and ask whether anyone lit a lamp for them.
- The exam system ended in 1905. Ask why your worth is still calculated the way an imperial bureaucracy calculated it.
- You were taught there is nothing here to leave. Ask why, then, it costs so much to disagree.


### closing

- Your tradition's actual texts are better than what was done with them. Confucius described relationships in both directions. Mencius said a ruler who fails his people forfeits the right to rule — and that a son must argue with a father who is wrong. The one-way version you inherited is a political edit, made by states that found reciprocity inconvenient.
- You can honor your parents and decline to be governed by them. You can care for them in old age and refuse to marry whom they choose. That is not the abandonment of filial piety. Read Mencius: it is the fulfillment of it, and the version you were taught is the counterfeit.

- His mother has found a tutoring centre for Mei. Mei is four. The centre is eleven thousand yuan a term and there is a waiting list and his mother has already spoken to someone about the list. She did not ask. She would say she did not need to ask, and in the framework they both live inside, she is correct.
- At work he stays until 8:40 because his manager is still there, and his manager stays because the director is still there, and nobody has ever articulated this arrangement, and everyone would describe it as commitment.
- At lunch his wife texts about her mother's hospital appointment and about who will take the day off. It will be her. It is always her. She is the daughter-in-law and this is not written down anywhere and it has never once been in question.
- His father calls at three about the second grandchild. Not directly — he mentions a cousin's second child, and the school it has got into, and the family's good fortune. Wei says mm. His father says he only mentions it because he wants Wei to be happy. His father means this entirely.
- At 11:20 he sits on the edge of the bed with his phone. He wants to say to somebody: I am tired, and I do not want the tutoring centre, and I would like one weekend that is mine. But there is nobody to say it to, because there is no organization to resign from and no doctrine to disbelieve and nobody has ever done anything but sacrifice for him — and so the only available shape for the sentence is *I am a bad son*, which is not what he means at all, and he cannot find the other shape, and eventually he plugs in his phone and lies down.



## Shinto
*East Asian*


### Opening

You may not consider yourself religious at all. You visit at New Year, you had your wedding at a shrine, and the whole thing feels like weather rather than belief — which is precisely why this profile matters. The single most dangerous religious capture in modern history happened here, in a tradition with no doctrine, no membership, and nothing anyone thought they were obeying.


### Overview

Japan's indigenous tradition of kami veneration, shrine practice, purification, and seasonal festival — largely non-doctrinal, non-congregational, and interwoven with Japanese cultural identity.


### Origin

Ancient localized kami cults; systematized alongside Buddhism; State Shinto (1868–1945) fused shrine religion with emperor worship and militarized nationalism — the modern era's clearest case of a tradition being weaponized by a state; postwar disestablishment returned shrines to private religious status.


### authority

- Shrine priesthood (often hereditary), the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honcho), neighborhood shrine communities.
- The political risk zone: shrine-network lobbying for constitutional revision and official Yasukuni patronage — re-entangling shrine and state. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT / ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### money

- Amulet and fortune sales, ceremony fees (blessings, weddings, groundbreakings), festival funding levies on neighborhoods, corporate purification services.
- The 'culture not religion' framing lets participation costs be socially levied without religious-freedom scrutiny. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### exit

- No membership to leave; costs are neighborly and reputational — opting out of shrine festivals or levies marks a household. [VARIES BY COMMUNITY]


### whoBenefits

- Hereditary shrine families; nationalist political networks borrowing sacred legitimacy; historically, the imperial state — the cautionary archetype for every church-state fusion in this codex. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### healthy

- Local shrine life as genuine commons: festivals, ecology, continuity without creed; priests and scholars resisting political capture of the tradition.


### timeline

- Prehistory–6th c. CE — Local kami veneration; no name, no canon, no clergy class — A landscape of local practice, not an organized religion.
- 6th–8th c. — Buddhism arrives; Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720) compiled — Myth is written down in service of imperial legitimacy — the first political use of the tradition.
- 9th–19th c. — Shinbutsu-shūgō: Shinto and Buddhism fused for a millennium — The tradition's boundaries are historically porous — 'pure Shinto' is a modern invention.
- 1868 — Meiji Restoration; forced separation of Shinto from Buddhism (shinbutsu bunri) — The state reorganizes religion by decree; Buddhist property destroyed.
- 1871–1945 — State Shinto: shrines nationalized, emperor worship compulsory, shrine attendance mandated — The clearest case in this codex of a tradition converted wholesale into a state coercion instrument. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- 1930s–1945 — Shrine rites integrated into militarism and colonial assimilation policy in Korea and Taiwan — Sacred ritual used to enforce imperial identity on subject populations. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1945–1946 — Occupation Shinto Directive disestablishes State Shinto; emperor renounces divinity — Religion is legally separated from the state and shrines become private bodies.
- 1946–present — Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honcho) organizes most shrines — A voluntary umbrella body with real political interests.
- 1969–present — Yasukuni Shrine visits by officials; Shinto Seiji Renmei lobbying for constitutional revision — Re-entanglement of shrine and state, contested in Japanese courts. [COURT RECORD]
- 2000s–present — Shrine mergers and rural depopulation; ritual tourism growth — Institutional contraction alongside commercial expansion.


### demographics

**adherents:** Jinja Honcho claims tens of millions of 'adherents' through household shrine affiliation; surveys show only a few percent of Japanese self-identify as Shinto believers. This is the largest counting discrepancy in the codex. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** Japan almost exclusively; ~80,000 shrines; small diaspora presence.

**branches:** Jinja (shrine) Shinto under Jinja Honcho, Sect Shinto (Tenrikyo and others historically classified separately), Folk and household Shinto, Imperial household rites.

**trend:** Rural shrines closing as villages depopulate; ritual participation persists as custom (New Year visits, weddings, groundbreaking) while belief claims stay very low.

**participation:** Most participants would deny being religious at all. The relevant control question here is not doctrine but social obligation — festivals, levies, and neighborhood expectation.


### info

- There is no doctrine to control, which makes 'this is culture, not religion' the tradition's structural deniability — and its historical use as a state instrument the reason to take it seriously anyway.
- Textbook and museum controversies over wartime history involve shrine-aligned political networks. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Yasukuni's on-site museum presents a contested account of the war; visits by officials carry the state's implicit endorsement. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### children

- Hatsumiyamairi (first shrine visit) and Shichi-Go-San mark childhood milestones — genuinely light-touch rites with no doctrinal enrollment.
- School participation in shrine visits and festivals has produced constitutional litigation over compelled religious activity. [COURT RECORD]
- Historically, State Shinto compelled schoolchildren to bow to the emperor's portrait and worship at shrines — coercion of children as state policy. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### gender

- Female priests exist and are numerous, though senior shrine leadership skews heavily male. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Menstrual and childbirth impurity (kegare) rules historically excluded women from certain rites and sacred spaces; some sites still bar women entirely. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Shrine-aligned political groups have campaigned against separate spousal surnames and for traditional family provisions in constitutional revision. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Hereditary priesthood transmits authority through families, ordinarily through sons.


### moneyTable

- Omamori amulets, ema plaques, omikuji fortunes — Blessing and protection — Retailed hope, purchased annually; a large and untaxed devotional economy — Shrines and shrine families
- Ceremony fees (weddings, purification, groundbreaking, car blessing) — Ritual services — Corporate and household purification contracts; commercial norms make refusal awkward — Shrines, and priests personally
- Neighborhood festival levies (chōnaikai collections) — Community festival costs — Household contributions collected by neighbors — refusal is socially visible and remembered — Local shrine and festival organizations [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Political lobbying by shrine associations — Cultural preservation — Devotional revenue supporting a constitutional-revision agenda most donors never voted on — Political networks [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### exitTable

- Formal membership — None — There is nothing to resign from; household affiliation is nominal — Accurately: there is no exit apparatus.
- Neighborhood standing — Yes — Declining festival levies or shrine duties marks a household as uncooperative — “It's a neighborhood association, not a church.”
- Family and ancestral duty — Yes — Refusing rites reads as disrespect to ancestors and parents — “It's just tradition.”
- Historical state coercion — Yes, 1871–1945 — Compulsory shrine worship, including in colonized Korea and Taiwan — “That was militarism, not Shinto.”


### whoPays

- Women, under purity exclusions and shrine-aligned family politics.
- Non-participating households in tight neighborhoods, socially marked.
- Japanese Christians and other minorities who resisted compulsory shrine worship — and were imprisoned for it. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Colonized Koreans and Taiwanese forced into shrine rites under assimilation policy.
- Anyone whose family history the Yasukuni narrative erases.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Very high deniability — No doctrine, no membership, no rules — nothing written to hold anyone to.
- Informal enforcement — Very high — Neighborhood expectation and family duty are the sole mechanisms today.
- Leadership distance — High — Jinja Honcho can disclaim any individual shrine, and shrines can disclaim politics.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Total — There is no doctrine at all — the ultimate ambiguity shield.
- Cultural outsourcing — Total — 'It is culture, not religion' is the tradition's own official self-description.
- Volunteer enforcement — Very high — Neighborhood associations and relatives collect and expect; no priest asks.
- Sacred secrecy — Medium — Imperial rites and some inner shrine practices are closed.
- Exit cost denial — High — Perfectly true institutionally; false at the level of the street you live on.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** State Shinto and emperor worship

**origin:** Constructed deliberately from 1868, nationalizing shrines and making imperial reverence compulsory; dismantled by directive in 1945. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

**thenPurpose:** A modernizing state needed a unifying loyalty for a population that had lived under regional lords. Local kami practice was reorganized into a national ideology from above.

**expired:** It ended in legal terms eighty years ago. Its lesson has not: this is the codex's clearest proof that a tradition with no doctrine and no clergy can still be converted into a total coercion instrument within one generation — precisely because there was nothing written to point at and say 'that is not what this says.'

**benefitsNow:** Historically, the imperial state and the military. Today, the political networks that campaign for constitutional revision using shrine legitimacy — and they benefit from your belief that none of this is religion. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]

**mechanism:** Neighborhood festival levies

**origin:** Community shrine support collected through neighborhood associations. [PATTERN OBSERVED]

**thenPurpose:** A village funding its own festival, where everyone participated and everyone benefited.

**expired:** In modern urban Japan, participation is voluntary in law and visible in practice. Declining is not a private act — it is a household decision your neighbors record. And because it is 'culture, not religion,' it evades the religious-freedom protections that would otherwise apply.

**benefitsNow:** Local shrine organizations, and social conformity generally. The 'culture not religion' framing is the mechanism: it lets a religious levy be collected without religious-liberty scrutiny.

**mechanism:** Purity exclusion of women (kegare)

**origin:** Ancient pollution concepts around blood and death. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Ritual ordering of sacred space in a pre-scientific framework.

**thenPurpose:** Honoring the dead — an obligation every culture recognizes.

**benefitsNow:** Nationalist political networks, who acquire a sacred venue where dissent looks like disrespect for the dead.

### leverage

- Shrine-aligned political organizations lobby for constitutional revision and traditional family provisions, converting devotional legitimacy into a policy agenda most participants never endorsed. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Under State Shinto, shrine rites were imposed on colonized Koreans and Taiwanese as assimilation policy — religion used as an instrument of imperial control over other peoples. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Corporate purification and groundbreaking contracts make shrine services a routine business expense, embedding religious practice in commercial life where refusal is awkward rather than illegal. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### hardQuestions

- If Shinto is culture and not religion, ask why the postwar constitution needed a clause separating it from the state.
- Ask whether your household could decline the festival levy for three years running and remain unremarked upon.
- Some shrines still bar women. Ask who decided, when, and on what authority — and note that nobody can tell you.
- Officials visit a shrine that enshrines convicted war criminals. Ask what a Korean or Chinese family is supposed to understand by that.
- In one generation this tradition was converted into compulsory emperor worship. Ask what structural feature made that possible — and whether it has changed.
- You were taught none of this is belief. Ask who benefits from a religion that cannot be criticized because it denies being one.


### closing

- Local shrine life is one of the genuinely good things in this codex: a commons, a calendar, trees kept standing, a place that belongs to everyone in the neighborhood and no one in particular. Almost nothing in this profile is aimed at that.
- What it is aimed at is the lesson of 1868 to 1945 — that a tradition with nothing written down is the easiest of all to hijack, because there is no text to hold up against the hijacker. Your protection is not doctrine; you have none. Your protection is remembering that it happened, and noticing who is currently standing near the torii with a political program.
