### day

**name:** Keiko

**when:** A Tuesday in autumn

**where:** A residential ward in Nagoya


**para**

- She hangs the washing before eight and greets Tanaka-san from next door, and the greeting is the whole architecture of her street compressed into four syllables and a bow of about fifteen degrees.
- The neighbourhood association envelope is on the shoe cupboard. Four thousand yen for the autumn festival. It is not a lot. It is not the point. The point is that Furukawa-san collects it in person, house by house, and that she has a list, and that the list is not a threat and does not need to be.
- Keiko is not religious. If a survey asked, she would say none. She goes to the shrine at New Year, she had her daughter blessed at one month, she will have a Buddhist funeral, and none of this feels like belief. It feels like being from here.
- At the school her son's class is visiting the shrine on Friday for a seasonal event. There is a form. A mother she knows slightly said last year that her family would prefer not to, and the teacher was very understanding, and the child went anyway, and nobody was unkind at any point in that sequence.
- In the afternoon on the news there is a story about a minister visiting a certain shrine, and a statement about it being in a private capacity, and a response from a neighbouring country. Keiko's mother, watching with her, says that the dead should be left in peace. Keiko's mother's uncle died in Burma in 1944 and is enshrined there, and Keiko has never once heard her mother say what she thinks about that.
- At night she puts the four thousand yen in the envelope and writes their family name on it in her good handwriting. She has done this every autumn for twenty-two years. It would not occur to her to describe any of it as religion, and it has never once occurred to her that she could decline — not because she is afraid, but because there is no available version of the sentence.



## Zoroastrianism
*Iranian*


### Opening

Your tradition put moral choice at the center of the universe before almost anyone else did — good thoughts, good words, good deeds, freely chosen. Which is why the mechanism at the heart of your community is so painful to look at: a rule that decides your child's religious existence based on which of their parents married out, and which sex that parent was.


### Overview

One of the world's oldest continuously practiced religions (~100–200K adherents: Parsis of India, Iranian Zoroastrians, diaspora); ethical dualism of good and evil, fire temples, and the triad of good thoughts, words, deeds.


### Origin

Prophet Zarathustra in ancient Iran (dating contested, ~2nd–1st millennium BCE); imperial religion of Persian empires; reduced to a minority under Islam; the Parsi migration to India built a prosperous, tightly-bounded community.


### authority

- Hereditary priesthood (only sons of priests may be ordained); community panchayats and trusts (notably the Bombay Parsi Punchayet) controlling housing, charity, and communal definition.
- The core control lever is boundary definition: who counts as Zoroastrian — patrilineal rules excluding intermarried women's children in the Parsi mainstream. [OFFICIAL POLICY: trust rules; litigated in Indian courts — COURT RECORD]


### money

- Enormous communal trusts and charitable endowments (housing colonies, hospitals, funds) — benevolence that is also leverage: access conditioned on communal standing and marriage choices. [COURT RECORD: BPP housing/intermarriage litigation]


### exit

- Intermarriage can cost temple access, communal housing, funerary rites (Towers of Silence), and children's initiation — exit penalties administered as boundary maintenance.


### whoBenefits

- Trust boards controlling assets and definitions; hereditary priesthood; the boundary itself concentrates power in its gatekeepers even as the community shrinks.


### healthy

- Reformist associations initiating children of intermarried women; Iranian Zoroastrian acceptance practices; the tradition's own ethic — free moral choice — as internal critique of coerced boundaries.


### timeline

- c. 1500–1000 BCE (contested) — Zarathustra's teaching in ancient Iran — Ethical dualism and individual moral choice — a foundation notably hostile to coercion.
- 550–330 BCE — Achaemenid Persian Empire — Royal patronage; the faith of a world empire.
- 224–651 CE — Sasanian Empire; Zoroastrianism as state religion with an organized priesthood — State church with heresy enforcement — the tradition's own high-control era. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 651–900 CE — Arab conquest; gradual conversion; jizya taxation of remaining Zoroastrians — From establishment to persecuted minority within two centuries.
- 8th–10th c. — Migration to Gujarat; the Parsi community forms — Survival strategy: tight endogamy and community boundary maintenance.
- 1600s–1800s — Parsi commercial prominence under Mughal and then British rule; Bombay Parsi Punchayet established — Enormous communal trusts created — benevolence with governance power. [FINANCIAL RECORD]
- 1800s — Priestly reform debates; Iranian Zoroastrians' jizya abolished 1882 — Reform currents emerge in both communities.
- 1900s — Demographic decline begins; intermarriage disputes intensify; global diaspora forms — Boundary questions become existential.
- 1908–present — Indian courts repeatedly adjudicate who counts as Parsi and who may use community facilities — The state is asked to rule on religious belonging. [COURT RECORD]
- 2000s–present — Population decline continues; reformist initiations of intermarried families' children; Iranian community pressures — The tradition faces its boundary question with its own survival at stake.


### demographics

**adherents:** ~110,000–200,000 worldwide — among the smallest traditions in this codex. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** India (Mumbai, Gujarat — the Parsi community, ~50,000–60,000 and falling), Iran (~15,000–25,000), plus North America, UK, Australia, Gulf states.

**branches:** Parsi (Indian) and Iranian Zoroastrian communities; reformist versus orthodox positions on conversion and intermarriage; Ilm-e-Kshnoom and other currents.

**trend:** Sustained decline: very low fertility, late marriage, high intermarriage, and — decisively — non-acceptance of intermarried women's children in the orthodox Parsi mainstream. Indian government funding has supported fertility programs for the community. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

**participation:** Community identity is exceptionally strong; institutional authority over housing, charity, and ritual access makes standing consequential in a way most small communities cannot match.


### info

- Priestly authority over ritual correctness; reformist priests who initiate children of intermarried mothers have faced sanction and exclusion from major fire temples. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Community disputes are largely public and litigated rather than concealed — an unusual degree of transparency, enforced by Indian courts. [COURT RECORD]
- Debate over Towers of Silence practice and reform is vigorous and open within the community.


### children

- Navjote initiation in childhood (typically 7–15) enrolls the child, and eligibility depends on parentage — a child's religious status is determined by which parent married out. [OFFICIAL POLICY: trust rules]
- Community schools, scholarships, and housing colonies build strong childhood identity and material dependence.
- Children of Parsi women who married non-Parsis have been refused navjote and temple entry by orthodox authorities — the harm lands on the child. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### gender

- The central inequality is patrilineal: a Parsi man's children by a non-Parsi wife are generally accepted, a Parsi woman's are generally not. Same act, different penalty by sex. [OFFICIAL POLICY / COURT RECORD]
- Menstrual seclusion practices persisted into the modern era and remain in some orthodox households. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Women are excluded from priesthood in Parsi practice; Iranian practice has seen some female religious instructors.
- The Bombay Parsi Punchayet's control over housing has meant intermarried women could lose access to community accommodation. [COURT RECORD]


### moneyTable

- Communal trusts and charitable funds (BPP and others) — Housing, healthcare, education, welfare — Access conditioned on communal standing and marriage choices — benevolence as boundary enforcement — Trust boards; and genuinely, community members in need [COURT RECORD]
- Housing colonies (baugs) — Affordable community housing — Subsidized housing withheld from those who marry out — the most concrete exit penalty here — Trust boards controlling allocation
- Ritual and funerary fees — Priestly services — Hereditary priesthood with limited numbers; funerary access is community-controlled — Priestly families and trusts
- Endowment investment income — Perpetual community support — Large historic endowments governed by small elected boards with contested legitimacy — Board members and their constituencies


### exitTable

- Ritual and temple access — Yes — Fire temple entry and funerary rites denied to those deemed outside the community — “These are religious requirements, not punishments.”
- Housing and welfare — Yes — Trust housing and benefits tied to communal standing — “Trust deeds specify beneficiaries.”
- Children's status — Yes — Navjote refused to children of intermarried mothers — “Descent rules are ancient.”
- Family and identity — Yes — In so small a community, exit means losing nearly everyone you know — “Nobody is shunned — they simply married out.”


### whoPays

- Parsi women who marry out — the single most clearly identifiable class of people harmed in this profile.
- Their children, denied initiation and temple access.
- Reformist priests sanctioned for performing those initiations.
- Iranian Zoroastrians, a persecuted minority under Islamic Republic law. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- The tradition itself, whose boundary rules are a documented driver of its own demographic decline.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Very low — Trust deeds and initiation rules are written and have been litigated in open court — the receipts are unusually complete.
- Informal enforcement — Medium — Community gossip and reputation supplement the formal rules.
- Leadership distance — Low — The Punchayet and named high priests make identifiable decisions — accountability is unusually traceable.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Medium — Reformists argue the scriptures support conversion and equality; orthodox authorities disagree, publicly.
- Cultural outsourcing — Medium — Framed as descent and heritage rather than religious rule.
- Volunteer enforcement — Medium — Family pressure around marriage is strong and constant.
- Sacred secrecy — Low — Non-Zoroastrians are excluded from some rites, but community governance is remarkably public.
- Exit cost denial — Low — The costs are documented in court filings — this community's harms are the best-evidenced and least deniable in the codex.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Patrilineal descent determining membership

**origin:** Community boundary rules hardened after the migration to India, as a tiny minority sought to survive within a Hindu majority. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Survival. A community of a few thousand under a foreign majority with no state protection maintained itself through strict endogamy. That reasoning was not paranoid; it worked for a millennium.

**expired:** The community is now declining fast, and the rule is a documented driver of that decline. It also produces an indefensible asymmetry: a man's children by an outsider are accepted, a woman's are not. Same act, opposite outcome, decided by sex. [COURT RECORD]

**benefitsNow:** Trust boards and orthodox authorities who control who counts — and gatekeepers gain power as the gate narrows, even while the community shrinks around them.

**mechanism:** Communal housing and welfare conditioned on standing

**origin:** Enormous charitable trusts built by prosperous Parsi families in the 18th–19th centuries: housing colonies, hospitals, funds. [FINANCIAL RECORD]

**thenPurpose:** Genuine and remarkable philanthropy — a community that took care of its poor better than almost any comparable group.

**expired:** When access is conditioned on communal standing and marriage choices, benevolence becomes enforcement. A woman who marries out can lose subsidized housing. That is not charity; it is a lever. [COURT RECORD]

**benefitsNow:** Trust boards, who control both the assets and the definitions that determine eligibility.

**mechanism:** Hereditary priesthood

**origin:** Priesthood restricted to sons of priestly families since antiquity. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Transmission of complex liturgical knowledge in a family-apprenticeship model.

**expired:** With a shrinking population, the priesthood shrinks faster — and heredity means the community cannot recruit ability from outside the priestly families. It is an inheritance structure limiting the supply of the very thing the community needs to survive.

**benefitsNow:** Priestly families' status and ritual monopoly. The cost is a liturgical tradition running out of practitioners.

**mechanism:** Funerary and temple access as boundary enforcement

**origin:** Purity requirements around fire temples and the Towers of Silence. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Ritual purity in a tradition with a highly developed purity framework.

**expired:** It now operates as the final sanction: an intermarried woman may be denied the rites for her own parents. Purity language performing a membership function.

**benefitsNow:** The boundary itself, and those who administer it.

### leverage

- Communal trusts control housing, healthcare, and welfare, and eligibility runs through communal standing — the clearest documented case in this codex of charity operating as a boundary-enforcement mechanism. [COURT RECORD]
- Indian courts have repeatedly been asked to adjudicate who counts as Parsi, which means the state has been enlisted into the community's internal boundary dispute. [COURT RECORD]
- Government-funded fertility programs have supported the community's demographic goals, tying public money to a reproduction agenda that the descent rule itself undermines. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### hardQuestions

- A Parsi man's children by an outsider are accepted; a Parsi woman's are not. Ask the high priest who says this is ancient to explain why the ancestor rule tracks the sex of the parent.
- If the community is dying, ask whether the rule that excludes its own grandchildren is preserving it or killing it. Then ask who keeps the rule anyway, and what they retain.
- Ask a trust board for the housing allocation criteria in writing. Note whether marriage appears.
- Reformist priests who initiate intermarried women's children have been sanctioned. Name what heresy they committed, using your own scriptures.
- Your religion's central claim is free moral choice. Explain a child excluded from the faith for a decision made before their birth.
- You were taught that criticism endangers a fragile community. Ask honestly which is doing more damage: the criticism, or the rule.


### closing

- Zarathustra's teaching is that a person chooses. That is not a peripheral doctrine in your tradition; it is the axis of the whole cosmology — the free mind selecting truth over falsehood. A membership rule based on parentage rather than choice contradicts the founding claim more directly than any critic could.
- There are reformists inside your community doing exactly this work: initiating the children, arguing the scriptures, losing standing for it. They are not abandoning the tradition. On the tradition's own terms, they may be the only ones fully practicing it.

### day

**name:** Freny

**when:** A Tuesday in Meher

**where:** A Parsi colony in Mumbai


**para**

- Sudreh and kusti at six, the knots and the words, and the fire in her mind that has been kept alight for three thousand years by people who chose to keep it alight. She is fifty-eight and she has never once found this boring.
- The flat is a trust flat. Two bedrooms, a fraction of market rent, in a colony with a hospital and a school and a fund for school fees. It is one of the most extraordinary charitable arrangements any community on earth has built, and her grandfather's generation built it, and she says so to anyone who will listen.
- Her daughter Zenobia married Rohan in 2019. Rohan is not Parsi. Zenobia's son Kayaan is three and has not had a navjote and will not have one, because Zenobia is the mother and not the father. If Freny's son had married a Hindu girl, the child would be initiated. Freny has done this arithmetic more times than she has done any other arithmetic in her life.
- At eleven she goes to the fire temple. Zenobia does not come. Zenobia has not come since 2019, and has never made a scene about it, and has simply stopped, which Freny finds harder than a scene.
- At lunch her neighbour mentions the housing list, and a case in the courts, and a priest in the suburbs who performs navjotes for children like Kayaan and who has been told not to. Freny says *hmm* and passes the dhansak. She has the priest's number in her phone. She has had it for two years.
- At night she sits by the window. She thinks: we are one hundred thousand people and we are getting fewer every year, and everyone says the community must survive. And then she thinks about a three-year-old who cannot enter the building where his great-grandfather's fire is kept, and she cannot make the two thoughts into one thought, and she has stopped expecting to.



## Baháʼí Faith
*Abrahamic-derived*


### Opening

You may have joined the least clerical religion in this codex — no priests, elected institutions, member-only funding, and a genuine record on race and gender that predates almost everyone else's. Most of what follows is not about your daily community life, which is likely warm and service-oriented. It is about the two or three mechanisms that activate the moment someone organizes a disagreement.


### Overview

~5–8 million members worldwide; a 19th-century religion teaching the oneness of God, religion, and humanity, with a global elected administrative order and no clergy.


### Origin

Founded by Baháʼu'lláh in 19th-century Iran/Ottoman exile out of the Bábí movement; leadership passed through appointed interpreters to the elected Universal House of Justice (1963); severely persecuted in Iran. [GOVERNMENT REPORT: UN documentation of Iranian persecution]


### authority

- Elected assemblies (local, national) under the Universal House of Justice; no campaigning, no clergy — and also no appeal beyond the system.
- The Covenant doctrine: unity enforced through the category of 'covenant-breaker,' whose adherents members must shun — the tradition's principal high-control mechanism. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Pre-publication review of members' writings about the Faith. [OFFICIAL POLICY]


### money

- Funds accept donations from members only (a genuine integrity feature); Huqúqu'lláh (19% on surplus wealth) paid to the Faith's center. [OFFICIAL POLICY]


### exit

- Ordinary resignation is administratively simple; the high cost is reserved for organized dissent — covenant-breaker designation severs even family association. [OFFICIAL POLICY / FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]
- Scholars publishing critical history have faced review pressure and disenrollment episodes. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY / ACADEMIC SOURCE — document specific cases before publication]


### whoBenefits

- The administrative order's continuity and narrative control; unity as institutional asset.
- Externally: the Iranian state benefits from persecuting Baháʼís as internal enemy — a reminder that this community is far more often victim than perpetrator of coercion. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### healthy

- No clergy, elected administration, member-only funding, and consultation ideals are real structural safeguards; most members experience a service-oriented, non-authoritarian community life.


### timeline

- 1844 — The Báb declares his mission in Shiraz — A messianic movement inside Shi'i Iran; thousands of followers killed in the ensuing persecution.
- 1863 — Baháʼu'lláh declares his prophetic station in Baghdad exile — The founding claim, made in exile and under state hostility.
- 1868–1892 — Imprisonment in Akka; writings composed; Covenant established — Succession is designated in writing specifically to prevent schism — an unusual founding safeguard.
- 1892–1921 — ʻAbduʼl-Bahá leads; Western expansion begins — The Faith becomes global and interracial early, well ahead of its era.
- 1921–1957 — Shoghi Effendi as Guardian; administrative order built — Elected institutions replace clergy — a deliberate structural anti-clericalism.
- 1957–1963 — Interregnum; Universal House of Justice first elected 1963 — Authority becomes fully institutional and elected; Covenant-breaker designations used against rival claimants. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1979–present — Islamic Republic persecution: executions, imprisonment, university exclusion, cemetery desecration — One of the most systematically persecuted religious minorities in the world today. [GOVERNMENT REPORT: UN Special Rapporteur reporting]
- 1980s–1990s — Bahá'í Institute for Higher Education founded after university bans; faculty arrested — A community builds an underground university because the state bars its youth from education. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- 1990s–2000s — Disputes over pre-publication review and academic freedom; some scholars disenrolled or resign — The tradition's internal control question surfaces around its own historians. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]
- 2000s–present — Ruhi/Institute process global expansion; continued Iranian persecution — Growth through structured study circles; persecution unabated.


### demographics

**adherents:** ~5–8 million claimed; independent estimates are lower and enrollment figures include inactive members. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** India (largest claimed population), Iran (historic center, now severely persecuted), United States, Kenya, DR Congo, Bolivia, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea.

**branches:** Overwhelmingly a single unified body — the Covenant structure has been unusually effective at preventing schism; small dissident groups (e.g., Orthodox Bahá'í) exist and are designated covenant-breakers.

**trend:** Steady but slower growth than mid-20th-century projections; large gap between enrollment rolls and active participation, acknowledged internally. [PATTERN OBSERVED]

**participation:** Enrollment counts overstate activity considerably. Most members experience a service-oriented, non-authoritarian community life; the high-control mechanisms activate almost exclusively around organized dissent.


### info

- Pre-publication review requires members to submit manuscripts about the Faith to institutional review before publishing — an explicit, written information control unusual among modern religions. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Covenant-breaker designation obliges members to shun the designated person entirely, including family — the sharpest sanction in the system. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Partisan political involvement is prohibited, which protects unity and also removes members from ordinary civic contestation. [OFFICIAL POLICY]


### children

- Children's classes and junior youth spiritual empowerment programs are central to the Institute process; participation is voluntary and typically warm.
- Declaration of faith at 15 is treated as the age of maturity — notably, an explicit age of consent for religious commitment, better than most traditions here. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- In Iran, Bahá'í children have faced school harassment and their families' businesses closed — harm imposed from outside, not within. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### gender

- Equality of men and women is explicit scripture and is practiced substantially in community life — one of the strongest positions in this codex.
- The exception: women are ineligible for the Universal House of Justice, the highest institution. Doctrinally unexplained, and the clearest internal inequality. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Chastity outside heterosexual marriage is required; same-sex marriage is not recognized, and LGBTQ members must remain celibate to stay in good standing. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Divorce is permitted after a year of patience — comparatively unrestrictive.


### moneyTable

- Bahá'í Funds (members-only contributions) — Support the Faith's work — Genuinely a safeguard: refusing outside money prevents donor capture — and giving amounts are confidential — The institutions; no individual clergy salary exists [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Huqúqu'lláh (19% of surplus wealth) — Right of God, paid to the Faith's head — A substantial obligatory payment, though privately assessed and not enforced by audit — The Universal House of Justice's funds
- Volunteer service and pioneering — Spread the Faith — Substantial unpaid labor and relocation expected of committed members — The institutional expansion plans
- Institute materials and training — Study circles — Modest costs; low commercial extraction compared with most traditions here — Publishing arms


### exitTable

- Ordinary resignation — Low cost — Administrative withdrawal; members generally retain relationships — Accurately: simple resignation is genuinely low-cost.
- Covenant-breaker designation — Severe — Total shunning including by immediate family, mandated by policy — “It's spiritual protection of unity, not punishment.”
- Loss of voting rights (administrative sanction) — Yes — For serious moral or covenant issues; membership without participation — “A remedial measure.”
- Scholarly cost — Documented cases — Review requirements and pressure on historians publishing critical work — “Review only checks accuracy of representation.”


### whoPays

- Iranian Bahá'ís — executed, imprisoned, and barred from higher education by the state. This community is far more often the victim of coercion than its author. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Designated covenant-breakers and their families, severed by policy.
- LGBTQ members, required to be celibate for life.
- Women, ineligible for the highest institution.
- Bahá'í scholars whose critical historical work met review pressure.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Very low — Shunning, review, and eligibility rules are all published — this tradition documents its own control mechanisms unusually openly.
- Informal enforcement — Medium — Community expectation around participation and unity discourse.
- Leadership distance — Low — Authority is clearly located in named elected institutions; accountability is traceable.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Low — Written scripture and interpretive authority are explicit; little room for retroactive reinterpretation.
- Cultural outsourcing — Low — Global and multi-ethnic; harms cannot easily be blamed on one culture.
- Volunteer enforcement — High — Shunning is carried out by ordinary members and relatives, as instructed.
- Sacred secrecy — Low — Institutional decisions on individuals are private, but doctrine and policy are public.
- Exit cost denial — Low — The Faith openly states what covenant-breaking entails — no denial is attempted.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Covenant-breaker designation and mandatory shunning

**origin:** Established in the Faith's early succession disputes to prevent the schisms that fractured earlier religions. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** A genuine and understandable problem: the founder watched rival claimants tear at the community and wrote in a mechanism to protect unity.

**expired:** It works — the Faith is unusually unified. But the price is a policy requiring members to sever contact with a designated person including their own family. Unity purchased by mandated shunning is not unity; it is the appearance of unity with the disagreement removed from view.

**benefitsNow:** The administrative order's continuity and narrative control. The cost is paid by designated individuals and by their relatives, who must choose.

**mechanism:** Pre-publication review

**origin:** Instituted as the Faith spread, to prevent inaccurate representations while it was small and widely misunderstood. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** A young religion facing hostile misrepresentation wanted its own accounts to be accurate. Defensible at the time.

**expired:** It is now an explicit, written requirement that members submit manuscripts about their own religion for institutional review before publishing — one of very few such systems in any modern religion. A faith that teaches independent investigation of truth cannot also vet the conclusions.

**benefitsNow:** Institutional control of the historical narrative. Scholars have reported pressure and disenrollment episodes over critical historical work. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]

**mechanism:** Exclusion of women from the Universal House of Justice

**origin:** Stated in the authoritative texts without explanation, in a religion whose central social teaching is the equality of men and women. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** No purpose is given. That is itself the notable fact.

**expired:** The Faith taught women's equality in 19th-century Iran, at real cost, and was right decades ahead of its neighbors. The single exclusion sits inside that record unexplained, which means it is defended by authority alone.

**benefitsNow:** Nothing identifiable, materially. It is the cleanest example in the codex of a rule sustained purely because questioning it is out of bounds.

**mechanism:** Prohibition on partisan political involvement

**origin:** Instituted to keep a global, multi-ethnic community from fracturing along national and factional lines. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Coherent and, in many contexts, protective — particularly for members under hostile governments.

**expired:** Partially: it also removes an entire community from ordinary civic contestation, including on matters affecting them, and it makes institutional direction the only permitted channel for collective action.

**benefitsNow:** Institutional unity, and in hostile states, arguably members' safety. This one is genuinely double-edged and the codex says so.

### leverage

- The clearest fact here runs the other way: the Iranian state persecutes Bahá'ís systematically — executions, imprisonment, exclusion from universities, cemetery desecration — using religion as an instrument against a defenseless minority. This community is far more often coercion's target than its author. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

- Huqúqu'lláh (19% of surplus wealth) flows to the Faith's central institutions, privately assessed, with no member-facing audit. [OFFICIAL POLICY]


### hardQuestions

- Your Faith teaches independent investigation of truth. Explain pre-publication review of members' writing about the Faith.
- If a designated covenant-breaker's family must shun them, ask which teaching about unity requires a mother to stop speaking to her son.
- Women's equality is central scripture. Ask an institution to explain the one exclusion without invoking its own authority.
- Ask for the accounting of Huqúqu'lláh. Note whether the question is answered or reframed as a spiritual matter.
- A scholar publishes accurate history the institutions dislike. Describe the process by which he is heard rather than removed.
- You were taught that unity is the highest value. Ask whether unity that requires shunning is unity or only silence.


### closing

- Your religion built real safeguards most traditions in this codex lack: no clergy, elected bodies, member-only funding, consultation as a method, and a documented history of getting race and gender right early and at cost. Those are not small. They are why this profile is short.
- But a faith confident in its own truth does not need to review what its historians write, and unity that requires a family to stop speaking is not the unity Baháʼu'lláh described — it is the appearance of it. Your tradition teaches you to investigate independently. That instruction was not meant to stop at the institutions' door.

### day

**name:** Sepideh

**when:** A Tuesday in Ayyám-i-Há

**where:** A city in Iran


**para**

- Prayers at dawn, alone, quietly, in a flat where the window faces a courtyard. Her grandmother taught her the Arabic. Her grandmother was in Evin for four years.
- She is twenty-two and cannot attend university. Not because of her marks — her marks were excellent — but because of the box on the form. She studies instead with the community's own institute, over patchy internet, with a lecturer in another city who has been arrested twice.
- At ten her father's shop is closed for the fourth time this year by an inspector who does not write anything down. Her father makes tea for the inspector. The inspector drinks it. This is how it goes.
- In the afternoon she teaches a children's class — six kids, a rug, songs about unity and the oneness of humanity, and she believes every word, and she has no idea how she would explain to a foreigner that this is the most dangerous thing she does all week.
- At six she reads an essay a Bahá'í academic abroad has written about the Faith's early history. It is careful and it is accurate and it has not been through review, and there was a note attached about that, and Sepideh does not know what she thinks. She thinks the essay is good. She thinks the review policy exists. She holds both.
- At night she and her mother count the cemetery. The graves were bulldozed in 2021 and it is not clear whether they will be allowed to bury her grandmother where her grandfather is. Sepideh prays for the officials by name, because the Writings say to, and she does it without irony, and then she lies down and thinks: everything trying to erase us is outside this room. That is true and it is nearly the whole story. Nearly.



## Mormonism / LDS
*Restorationist Christian*


### Opening

You may have felt something in a testimony meeting that has never left you, and you may have a family you love organized entirely around this. Read the next part anyway, because there is one fact you were funding for sixty-four years and were not permitted to see — and a federal regulator, not an enemy of the Church, is the one who documented it.


### Overview

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, ~17 million members on the rolls; a 19th-century American restorationist faith with living prophets, lay clergy, temple covenants, and a famously organized global structure.


### Origin

Founded by Joseph Smith (1830, upstate New York) on new scripture and prophetic authority; Brigham Young's Utah settlement built a church-state; the 20th century corporatized the institution into one of the wealthiest religious bodies per capita on earth.


### authority

- Strict hierarchy: prophet and apostles (lifetime, self-perpetuating) → stake presidents → bishops; worthiness interviews (including of minors, historically with sexually explicit questions — a reform pressure point [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]) gate temple access.
- Correlation: centralized control of all curriculum and messaging. [OFFICIAL POLICY]


### money

- Tithing (10%) linked directly to temple worthiness — salvation-gated revenue. [OFFICIAL POLICY: temple recommend questions]
- Ensign Peak Advisors: whistleblower disclosure (2019) revealed a reserve fund exceeding $100 billion built from tithing surplus; in 2023 the SEC fined the Church and Ensign Peak $5 million for using shell LLCs to obscure the portfolio's size for over 20 years. [FINANCIAL RECORD / GOVERNMENT REPORT: SEC administrative order, Feb 2023]
- Members' rolls-based statistics overstate activity; finances are undisclosed to the members who fund them. [PATTERN OBSERVED / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### exit

- Family strain in multigenerational LDS families; loss of temple participation in relatives' weddings; social-professional costs in the Mormon corridor; missionary-age youth face identity-scale exit decisions.
- Resignation was historically obstructed; formalized processes (and QuitMormon legal service) emerged under pressure. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]


### whoBenefits

- The corporate church: a self-perpetuating leadership controlling a nine-figure-plus portfolio with zero member-facing financial disclosure since 1959 (U.S.). [FINANCIAL RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Church-owned commercial arms (real estate, media, agribusiness — e.g., City Creek mall development funded amid tithing rhetoric). [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### healthy

- Genuine welfare and disaster-relief operations; lay ministry involving members deeply; reform pressure from faithful members (financial transparency advocates, interview-policy reformers) demonstrating loyal dissent.


### timeline

- 1820–1830 — Joseph Smith's visions; Book of Mormon published; Church organized 1830 — New scripture plus living prophetic authority — a claim that makes present leadership unchallengeable.
- 1831–1844 — Kirtland, Missouri, Nauvoo; polygamy introduced secretly; Smith killed 1844 — Secret doctrine practiced by leadership while publicly denied — the founding instance of a pattern. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1846–1857 — Brigham Young leads migration to Utah; theocratic territorial government — A church that is also a state, an economy, and a court system.
- 1857–1890 — Federal conflict over polygamy; 1890 Manifesto ends the practice officially — Doctrine reversed under state pressure and reframed as revelation. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1890–1950 — Assimilation; tithing systematized; welfare program built — Institutional consolidation and financial discipline.
- 1959 — Church ceases publishing financial statements to members (U.S.) — Members fund an institution whose books they may no longer see. [FINANCIAL RECORD]
- 1978 — Revelation ends the racial priesthood and temple ban — A doctrine held for over a century is reversed; the prior teaching later disavowed. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1980s–2000s — Correlation centralizes all curriculum; excommunication of the 'September Six' (1993) — Historians and intellectuals disciplined for research. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- 2013–2019 — Gospel Topics essays acknowledge polygamy, race, and translation issues; 2015 exclusion policy on LGBTQ families, reversed 2019 — Transparency under internet pressure; a major policy reversed within four years. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 2019–2023 — Whistleblower reveals Ensign Peak's $100B+ reserve; SEC fines Church and Ensign Peak $5M (Feb 2023) for shell-company concealment — A federal regulator documents two decades of deliberate obfuscation. [GOVERNMENT REPORT: SEC order]
- 2018–present — Worthiness-interview reform campaigns; abuse-reporting litigation over the clergy helpline — Internal reform pressure from believing members. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### demographics

**adherents:** ~17.2 million on the rolls; independent analyses estimate active participation at roughly a third of that, and self-identification in national surveys is far lower than official counts. [OFFICIAL POLICY: Church statistical report / ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** United States (~6.7M, concentrated in Utah, Idaho, Arizona, Nevada, California), Mexico, Brazil, Philippines, Peru, Nigeria, and a large missionary-driven Global South presence.

**branches:** The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (the overwhelming majority); Community of Christ (formerly RLDS); fundamentalist polygamous groups (FLDS and others) that the main church disavows.

**trend:** Growth has slowed markedly; retention of youth in the U.S. has declined; membership rolls include many inactive and unlocatable members, which the Church acknowledges only indirectly. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**participation:** The rolls/activity gap is one of the largest in this codex — members are recorded from baptism and rarely removed, so official counts substantially overstate the population under institutional authority.


### info

- Correlation gives headquarters control over every lesson manual, magazine, and curriculum item worldwide. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- For decades, difficult history (polygamy's scope, the race ban's origins, translation methods) was absent from Church curricula; the Gospel Topics essays (2013–) acknowledged much of it only after the internet made concealment untenable. [OFFICIAL POLICY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Members were counseled against 'anti-Mormon' material, and historians who published on sensitive topics were excommunicated in 1993. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- The abuse-reporting helpline routes bishops to Church attorneys, a structure litigated as prioritizing institutional liability over child protection. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### children

- Baptism at age 8 — designated the 'age of accountability' — enrolls children into covenants and tithing expectations before adolescence.
- One-on-one worthiness interviews of minors by adult male leaders, historically including sexually explicit questioning, are the sharpest child-safeguarding issue here and the target of an active reform campaign. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Youth are expected to plan for missions from childhood; missionary service at 18–19 involves surrendered communication, assigned companions, and controlled schedules at a formative age.
- Temple garments, chastity teaching, and 'For the Strength of Youth' standards regulate dress and dating from early adolescence.


### gender

- Priesthood is male-only; every governing office above the local women's organization is held by men. Women's Relief Society leadership operates under male priesthood oversight. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Kate Kelly was excommunicated in 2014 for advocating women's ordination — a documented case of dissent penalized. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Temple ceremony language historically had women covenant differently than men; revisions in 2019 reduced but did not eliminate the asymmetry. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- LGBTQ members: the 2015 policy labeled same-sex married members apostates and barred their children from baptism; reversed in 2019 after documented family harm. Same-sex marriage remains grounds for loss of standing. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Chastity teaching has been linked by former members to lasting sexual shame, with worthiness interviews as the enforcement mechanism. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]


### moneyTable

- Tithing (10% of income) — Fund the Church's work — Directly linked to temple recommend worthiness — access to the highest ordinances, including family sealings, is conditioned on payment. This is salvation-gated revenue, and it is written policy. [OFFICIAL POLICY] — The corporate church and its investment arms
- Ensign Peak Advisors reserve fund — Prudent reserves for future needs — $100B+ accumulated from tithing surplus, concealed through shell LLCs for over 20 years until an SEC enforcement action — The institution; members were never told [GOVERNMENT REPORT: SEC order, Feb 2023]
- Missionary self-funding — Serve a mission — Families pay for their own children's unpaid full-time labor — the Church's largest workforce funds itself — The institution's growth operations
- Commercial holdings (real estate, agribusiness, media, City Creek) — Stewardship of assets — Members were asked to sacrifice for a mall development amid tithing rhetoric — The corporate church [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Unpaid lay clergy and member labor — Service — Enormous operational cost savings with no member equity; leaders at the top do receive stipends — The institution


### exitTable

- Family relationships — Yes — Multigenerational family identity; exclusion from temple weddings of relatives; parental grief framing — “Families are eternal — leaving is the member's own choice.”
- Community and employment — Yes in the Mormon corridor — Social and professional networks overlap heavily with the ward; BYU honor-code enforcement affects students and staff — “Employment standards apply to everyone who agreed to them.”
- Records and resignation — Historically obstructed — Resignation requests once routed through local leaders; legal services (QuitMormon) emerged to force removal — “Members may withdraw at any time.”
- Eternal-family threat — Yes — Leaving is taught to jeopardize eternal sealing to spouse and children — the highest-stakes spiritual threat in this codex — “It's doctrine about consequences, not coercion.”


### whoPays

- Children interviewed alone about their sexuality by adult male leaders.
- Abuse survivors whose reports were routed through a legal-liability helpline. [COURT RECORD]
- Women, excluded from all governing authority and disciplined for advocating inclusion.
- LGBTQ members and their children, especially under the 2015–2019 policy.
- Poor tithe-payers, for whom 10% is the difference between rent and eviction, while $100B sat in reserve.
- Missionaries' families, self-funding two years of unpaid institutional labor.
- Members who gave decades of money to books they were not permitted to see.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Very low — The General Handbook, temple recommend questions, and financial policies are written — tithing-for-temple-access is documented policy, not inference.
- Informal enforcement — High — Ward social standing, callings, and family expectation do most of the day-to-day work.
- Leadership distance — Medium — Correlation centralizes messaging, which makes deniability harder — but local leader discretion absorbs blame for individual harm.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Medium — 'Policy, not doctrine' is used to reverse positions (race ban, 2015 policy) without acknowledging error.
- Cultural outsourcing — Medium — Harms attributed to Utah culture or overzealous local leaders rather than to structure.
- Volunteer enforcement — High — Unpaid lay leadership means neighbors conduct the interviews and the discipline.
- Sacred secrecy — Low — Temple covenants are secret, and financial reporting was concealed — both documented, the latter by federal regulators.
- Exit cost denial — High — 'Nobody is holding you here' — said by an institution that teaches your family is eternal only through it.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Tithing linked to temple worthiness

**origin:** Tithing formalized in the 19th century; the temple recommend interview system linked payment to access as the institution consolidated. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** A destitute frontier community pooling resources to build settlements, irrigation, and temples. Everyone could see where the money went — it was the wall going up outside.

**expired:** Visibility ended in 1959, when the Church stopped publishing financial statements to U.S. members. The link between payment and access did not end. You are asked for ten percent, told your family's eternal sealing depends on it, and refused the books.

**benefitsNow:** The corporate church and its investment arms. A whistleblower revealed a reserve exceeding $100 billion accumulated from tithing surplus, and in 2023 the SEC fined the Church and Ensign Peak $5 million for using shell companies to conceal it for over twenty years. [GOVERNMENT REPORT: SEC order]

**mechanism:** Worthiness interviews of minors

**origin:** Developed through the 20th century as bishops became the local gatekeepers of temple access and standing. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Pastoral oversight in small frontier wards where the bishop was the community's known and accountable leader.

**expired:** It means an untrained adult male volunteer questions a child alone about their sexual thoughts and behavior, with the child's standing in their family's religion depending on the answers. Reform campaigns run by believing members target exactly this. No other institution that works with children would permit this structure.

**benefitsNow:** Institutional control of sexual conformity, enforced without paid staff. The cost is borne by children, and by adults who report lasting sexual shame. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]

**mechanism:** Correlation — total centralization of curriculum

**origin:** Built from the 1960s–70s to standardize teaching materials worldwide. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Consistency across a rapidly globalizing church, and quality control over lesson content.

**expired:** It produced a system in which difficult history — polygamy's scope, the origins of the race ban, translation methods — was absent from every official source until the internet made concealment impossible. The Gospel Topics essays from 2013 conceded material members had been told was anti-Mormon lies.

**benefitsNow:** Institutional narrative control. And note the sequence: the disclosure followed the exposure. It was not led.

**mechanism:** 'Policy, not doctrine' reversibility

**origin:** Prophetic authority combined with continuing revelation permits reversal without error. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** A living church able to receive new light — a genuine theological strength.

**expired:** In practice it means positions held for over a century (the racial priesthood ban) or four years (the 2015 policy excluding children of same-sex couples from baptism) can be reversed without anyone being wrong, and without accounting to the families harmed in between.

**benefitsNow:** Leadership, which retains infallibility while changing positions. The cost was paid by Black members for 126 years and by LGBTQ families for four.

### leverage

- The $100 billion-plus Ensign Peak reserve was accumulated from tithing surplus and concealed through shell LLCs for over two decades until the SEC's 2023 enforcement action. Members funded it, were told to sacrifice for it, and were never shown it. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Church-funded political campaigns — most visibly California's Proposition 8 — mobilized member money and volunteer labor into legislation affecting non-members' civil status. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Missionary labor is self-funded: families pay for their own children's two years of unpaid full-time work for the institution. The largest workforce in the Church funds itself. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- The abuse-reporting helpline routes bishops to Church attorneys rather than to police; litigation has argued this structure prioritized institutional liability over children. [COURT RECORD]


### hardQuestions

- A federal regulator fined your Church for hiding a $100 billion portfolio from the people who funded it. Ask why the disclosure required a regulator, and ask which leader was held accountable.
- If tithing is a spiritual principle, ask why access to your daughter's sealing depends on your having paid it.
- Why does an untrained volunteer question a twelve-year-old alone about masturbation, and what institution that works with children would call that acceptable?
- Material the Church now publishes was called anti-Mormon lies when members raised it. Ask whether the historians excommunicated in 1993 have been reinstated and thanked.
- The 2015 policy was revelation, then reversed in 2019. Ask what happened to the families in between, and who apologized to them.
- If a bishop learns a child is being abused and calls a Church attorney instead of the police, ask plainly who that call was protecting.


### closing

- Your own scripture says a prophet is only a prophet when acting as such, and your own tradition insists you seek personal confirmation rather than take a leader's word. That is not a loophole. It is the mechanism your religion gave you for exactly this situation, and the people using it — the transparency advocates, the interview reformers, the members who forced the essays — are not enemies of the Church. They are the reason it changed at all.
- You can keep the family, the covenants, and the God, and refuse to fund an institution that will not show you the ledger. Asking a question is not apostasy. And if a hundred billion dollars had to be hidden from you for twenty years, the honest question is not whether you are worthy of the temple. It is whether they were worthy of your paycheck.

### day

**name:** Kimberly

**when:** A Tuesday in November

**where:** Utah County


**para**

- Scriptures at 5:45 before the four kids are up, because that is when it can happen. Her testimony is not fragile and it is not borrowed. It is the load-bearing wall of her life and she has checked.
- Tithing settlement is coming in December. Ten percent of Brad's gross, which is $6,100 this year, which is also the transmission and the orthodontist. She will pay it, and they will find the money, and she will sit across from Bishop Anderson — who is a good man who sells insurance — and confirm that she is a full tithe payer, and he will sign the recommend.
- Her niece Sadie is getting married in the temple in March. Kimberly's brother Doug does not have a recommend. He will wait in the lobby during his own daughter's sealing. Nobody in the family says anything about this and everybody thinks about it constantly.
- At eleven she takes a casserole to a sister in the ward who just had a baby, and stays forty minutes, and it is the best thing either of them does that week, and Kimberly wants this on the record too, because it is not decoration. It is what the Church is for and it works.
- In the afternoon her son Cole, who is twelve, has an interview with the bishop. Alone. It is standard. Kimberly sits in the foyer and thinks about the questions she was asked at twelve, and about the fact that she cannot remember whether she was asked them or whether she is remembering someone else's account, and about the specific quality of not wanting to know.
- At ten she is on her phone and there is an article about the Ensign Peak settlement — a hundred billion dollars, twenty years, shell companies, five million dollar penalty. She reads it twice. She puts the phone down. She thinks about the transmission and the orthodontist and about the December meeting, and about the fact that in December nobody will ask Bishop Anderson anything, and that he could not answer it if she did, and that the only person in the entire arrangement who will be asked a question is her.



## Seventh-day Adventism
*Abrahamic — Christian (Adventist)*


### Opening

If your health, your education, and your community all came from this church, the ledger genuinely does have large entries on the credit side, and this page does not pretend otherwise — the Adventist hospital and school systems are real institutions doing real good. What follows examines two specific things: an authority claim that cannot be tested, and the machinery that has been used against members who tried to test it anyway.


### Overview

A global Protestant denomination of roughly 22 million members, founded in the aftermath of a failed 1844 date-setting prophecy, distinguished by Saturday Sabbath observance, a health and vegetarianism tradition, one of the world's largest Protestant education and hospital systems, and the prophetic authority of its co-founder Ellen G. White.


### Origin

Adventism was born from a specific, dated, public failure. William Miller and his followers taught that Christ would return in 1844; on 22 October that year, tens of thousands of people gave away property, settled debts, and waited. Nothing happened. It is called the Great Disappointment, and it is the movement's honest name for it. What followed is the movement's founding intellectual act: rather than abandoning the date, a group reinterpreted it — Christ had not returned to earth but had entered the heavenly sanctuary to begin an 'investigative judgment.' The event was relocated from the visible world to an invisible one, where it could not be checked. Ellen G. White's visions confirmed the reinterpretation, and her prophetic authority became the movement's load-bearing wall. From that beginning grew something genuinely remarkable: a worldwide health, education, and publishing network, a vegetarian tradition that anticipated modern nutrition science by a century, and a Loma Linda population that appears in longevity research as one of the world's healthiest communities.


### day

**name:** Marisol

**when:** A Friday in September

**where:** Loma Linda, California


**para**

- She closes her laptop at four so the Sabbath does not catch her working, and there is a real peace in that, the kind of peace you cannot buy — a full day where nobody can ask her for anything. She would not trade it. She knows people who envy it and she thinks they are right to.
- Her father worked forty years at the hospital and her mother taught at the academy. The tithe went to the conference every month of her childhood and she has never once seen a figure for what the conference did with it, and it has never once occurred to her to ask, and she notices this week that those two facts sit next to each other oddly.
- In Sabbath School someone asks about the investigative judgment — about whether the 1844 date really means what the pioneers said it meant. The teacher says it is settled and moves on, warmly, and the room relaxes, and Marisol notices that the relaxing is the answer.
- She looks up Desmond Ford that afternoon, because the name came up once and nobody explained it. A theologian, a hearing at a place called Glacier View in 1980, his ministerial credentials withdrawn. She reads that he kept attending Adventist churches for the rest of his life. She does not know what to do with that and she does not close the tab.
- Her cousin's wife is a pastor in a union that ordains women, and the General Conference voted in 2015 that it may not, and there are committees about compliance now, and at family dinner nobody mentions it while everybody knows. Marisol thinks: we have a word for a room where everyone knows and nobody says. She does not say the word.
- At sundown they sing, and the singing is genuinely beautiful, and her father's face is the face of a man who is where he belongs. Marisol wants that. She also wants to know what happened at Glacier View. She has not yet worked out whether those are two wants or one.



### timeline

- 22 October 1844 — The Great Disappointment — the Millerite date passes and Christ does not return — The movement's founding falsification, publicly acknowledged. What the movement did next is the subject of the rest of this page.
- 1844–1850s — Hiram Edson's sanctuary insight; the investigative-judgment doctrine forms; Ellen White's visions begin and confirm it — A failed prediction is relocated to an unobservable realm. The claim survives by becoming untestable — the single most important structural move in this tradition. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1863 — The General Conference of Seventh-day Adventists is organized in Battle Creek, Michigan — The movement chooses representative structure with elected officers — the decision that gives this tradition a genuinely removable apex, unlike most pages in this codex.
- 1866–1900s — The Western Health Reform Institute becomes the Battle Creek Sanitarium under John Harvey Kellogg; the health message spreads — The credit side of the ledger begins: a real and early contribution to nutrition, sanitation, and preventive medicine.
- 1907 — Kellogg is expelled from the church after doctrinal and institutional conflict; Battle Creek is lost — The first demonstration that the structure would separate from its most famous institution rather than lose control of doctrine.
- 1919 — The Bible Conference debates the nature of Ellen White's inspiration; the transcripts are then filed away and not published for decades — Leaders privately discussed the limits of the prophetic claim and did not tell the members. The transcripts resurfaced in the 1970s. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1970s — Merikay Silver's equal-pay litigation against Pacific Press; the church's denominational pay practices are challenged in US federal court — A member used civil law against the institution's employment practice and the courts engaged. [COURT RECORD]
- 1980 — Glacier View: theologian Desmond Ford challenges the investigative-judgment doctrine and has his ministerial credentials withdrawn — The tradition's clearest documented case of what happens to a credentialed insider who tests the load-bearing claim in public. Ford attended Adventist churches for the rest of his life. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1982 — Walter Rea publishes The White Lie, documenting extensive unattributed literary borrowing in Ellen White's writings; a church-commissioned study by Fred Veltman later confirms substantial dependence in The Desire of Ages — The institution's own commissioned research confirmed the substance of a critic's charge — a genuinely creditable act, and one whose implications for the prophetic claim were never squarely faced in public. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1980s — The Davenport affair: church entities lose substantial funds in the collapse of a member's investment scheme; internal reviews follow — A financial failure that forced the first serious conflict-of-interest rules on denominational officers. [FINANCIAL RECORD]
- 2015 — The General Conference session in San Antonio votes against allowing divisions to authorize the ordination of women — A representative body voted, which is more than most institutions in this codex can say — and it voted to keep an exclusion that several of its own unions had already ended.
- 2016–2018 — 'Compliance' committees are established to address unions ordaining women; the mechanism is contested across the church's own governance bodies — The apparatus turns inward on its own elected regional bodies — accountability machinery used to enforce rather than to examine.
- 2025 — The General Conference session elects Erton Köhler as president, succeeding Ted N. C. Wilson after fifteen years — A peaceful, contested, scheduled transfer of the highest office. Almost nowhere else in this codex does that sentence appear. (Verify current officers before citing.)


### demographics

**adherents:** Roughly 22 million baptized members worldwide, with the church's own reporting acknowledging a substantial gap between baptisms recorded and members retained. [OFFICIAL POLICY: GC statistical report]

**regions:** Overwhelmingly Global South: Africa (the largest bloc by far), Latin America, the Philippines, and India, with historically significant but proportionally small memberships in North America, Europe, and Australia.

**branches:** One unified worldwide organization under the General Conference, plus historical offshoots — Davidians and Branch Davidians among them — which the church disavows and which are frequently and unfairly used to characterize it.

**trend:** Growing fast in Africa and Latin America; roughly flat or declining in North America and Europe. The church's own audits have repeatedly found large numbers of members recorded but not retained.

**participation:** Sabbath observance makes participation unusually visible and unusually costly — it structures employment, schooling, and social life in a way weekly attendance elsewhere does not.


### authority

- The General Conference in session is the highest authority, and it is genuinely representative: delegates from around the world elect the president and officers at a session held roughly every five years, and the office has changed hands by vote. On the codex's central question — who can remove the person at the top — this tradition answers better than nearly every other page here, and that should be said plainly.
- Beneath the vote sits a claim that no vote reaches: Ellen G. White's writings are held as the 'lesser light,' authoritative but subordinate to scripture. In practice her writings settle disputes, and a member who challenges their authority is challenging the movement's foundation rather than an opinion.
- The 28 Fundamental Beliefs are the doctrinal boundary, and ministerial credentials are held by conferences and unions — which is where the real disciplinary power sits, and where Desmond Ford's was withdrawn.

### money

- Tithe here is unusually structured and unusually opaque at the point where it matters. Ten percent goes not to the local congregation but upward to the conference, which pays pastors' salaries; the local church is funded separately by offerings. That means the money a member gives is deliberately separated from the church they can see, and pastoral employment depends on a body the congregation does not control.
- The system is professionally audited by the General Conference Auditing Service, and summary financial reports are produced — this is real, and it puts the tradition ahead of most in this codex. What is not routinely available to an ordinary member is a plain, local answer to a plain question: how much did this congregation send upward last year, and what specifically was it spent on.
- The health and education systems are enormous revenue enterprises. Their governance is corporate, their relationship to church governance is intricate, and executive compensation in the hospital systems is the single most reliably under-discussed number in Adventist life.
- Adventist Development and Relief Agency work is substantial and independently evaluated in many jurisdictions — a genuine and checkable credit entry.


### moneyTable

- Tithe (10%) — Supporting the worldwide gospel work through the conference — Medium — the flow is upward and away from local visibility, and it pays the salary of the pastor the congregation did not hire — The conference and union structures
- Local church budget offerings — Running the congregation you actually attend — Low — visible, local, and usually reported to the members — The local congregation
- Church school tuition — Educating children in the faith — Medium — a substantial recurring cost, and a strong retention mechanism as well as a genuine service — The education system
- Health system revenue — Hospital and clinic operations — Medium — large corporate entities whose executive pay is rarely surfaced to members — The health corporations and their executives
- Publishing and literature evangelism — Spreading the message and employing colporteurs — Medium — a sales workforce paid on commission, historically with weak labour protections — The publishing houses
- ADRA and disaster offerings — Relief and development — Low — independently evaluated in many jurisdictions and among the more checkable flows in this codex — Beneficiaries, substantially and verifiably


### genealogy

**mechanism:** The investigative judgment

**origin:** Formed in 1844–45 to explain why a publicly announced date had passed with nothing visible happening.

**thenPurpose:** It rescued a devastated community. Thousands of people had given away everything and needed a way to understand the day after — and the reinterpretation gave the disappointment meaning rather than ridicule.

**expired:** It works by relocating the event to a place no one can look. A claim built specifically to be unobservable cannot be tested, and when a credentialed theologian tested it anyway in 1980, the response was to withdraw his credentials rather than answer him.

**benefitsNow:** The doctrinal structure and the offices that rest on it. A doctrine that cannot be checked cannot be lost, and the people who administer it cannot be wrong.

**mechanism:** Prophetic authority — the writings of Ellen G. White

**origin:** Visions beginning in 1844 that confirmed the sanctuary reinterpretation and shaped doctrine, diet, education, and health practice.

**thenPurpose:** Cohesion and direction for a scattered, humiliated movement with no leaders, no institutions, and no reason to expect survival. Her health counsel was, in substance, decades ahead of the medicine of her time.

**expired:** The church's own commissioned research confirmed extensive literary dependence in her writings. That finding — creditably published — was never squarely reconciled with the authority claim built on them, and the claim continued unchanged.

**benefitsNow:** Whoever cites her to close a discussion. An unreviewable authority is most useful to the person invoking it, which is why it appears at the end of arguments rather than the start.

**mechanism:** Tithe flowing upward to the conference

**origin:** Nineteenth-century systematic benevolence, designed so that poor congregations could still have trained pastors.

**thenPurpose:** Genuine solidarity: a rich church's tithe paid for a poor church's pastor, which is a good idea and worked.

**expired:** The solidarity mechanism became a control mechanism. Pastors are employed by the body that receives the money, not the congregation that gives it, so a pastor's livelihood is structurally independent of the people they serve and structurally dependent on the office above them.

**benefitsNow:** Conference and union administration. The mechanism's original beneficiaries — poor congregations — still benefit; so does every officer whose authority over pastors runs through payroll.

**mechanism:** The parallel institution system

**origin:** Schools, sanitariums, and publishing houses built because Adventists were excluded from, or unwilling to use, the surrounding society's institutions.

**thenPurpose:** Survival and service for a Sabbath-keeping minority that could not take Saturday examinations or Saturday shifts.

**expired:** The exclusion has largely ended; the parallel world has not. A member can now be born, schooled, employed, treated, and buried entirely inside the system — which converts a shelter into an enclosure, and makes leaving a career decision as much as a spiritual one.

**benefitsNow:** The institutional system, which is also one of the largest Protestant employers on earth. Every exit cost on this page runs through it.


### info

- The 1919 Bible Conference transcripts, in which leaders candidly discussed the limits of Ellen White's inspiration, were filed and effectively unavailable to members for roughly half a century. Members were not told what their leaders had said among themselves. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- The Veltman study, commissioned by the church, confirmed substantial literary dependence in The Desire of Ages. Commissioning it was creditable; its findings have never been integrated into how the prophetic claim is taught to ordinary members.
- The denominational press is substantial and the independent Adventist press — publications and forums run by members — is genuinely lively and critical. That independent sector is a real strength and is worth naming as one.
- Church school curricula present the movement's history in a form in which the 1919 conference, the Veltman findings, and Glacier View are largely absent.


### children

- The church school system is extensive and often academically strong; it is also the primary retention mechanism, and tuition is a significant recurring cost.
- Children are taught the investigative judgment — a doctrine in which one's life is under review in a heavenly court — at ages where it reliably produces scrupulosity. This is among the most consistently reported harms in former-member accounts. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY]
- End-time and persecution teaching aimed at children produces documented anxiety, particularly around the 'time of trouble' and Sunday-law scenarios.
- Sabbath observance shapes a child's entire social world — no Saturday sport, no Saturday activities — which builds a strong in-group and a narrow out-group by design.


### gender

- Women were central from the founding: the movement's most authoritative voice was a woman, and Adventism ran on female labour, teaching, and writing from the beginning.
- The world church nevertheless voted in 2015 not to permit divisions to authorize women's ordination, and then created compliance machinery aimed at the regional bodies that had already done so. The founder's authority is unquestionable; women holding the founder's kind of authority is not.
- Merikay Silver's litigation in the 1970s established that denominational employment practices could be examined in a civil court — a member forcing the question the institution would not answer internally. [COURT RECORD]
- Modesty and health teaching are applied more intensively to women's bodies than to men's, and diet culture inside Adventism can shade into disordered eating in ways the health message is not equipped to notice.

### exit

- Leaving is legally free and, in the concentrated communities, occupationally expensive: where the hospital, the university, and the school are all Adventist, a change of belief can be a change of career.
- There is no shunning doctrine and no formal disfellowshipping for simple non-attendance — an important and creditable difference from several neighbouring pages in this codex. The cost is social, familial, and professional rather than mandated.
- The heaviest reported burden is internal: an end-time framework and an investigative-judgment doctrine absorbed in childhood do not switch off when attendance stops, and health anxiety around diet often outlives belief.


### exitTable

- Employment — Sometimes — In Loma Linda, Andrews, and similar concentrations, the church system is the major employer — “Employment is governed by ordinary policy, not belief.”
- Family closeness — Sometimes — Sabbath structures family life; a leaver becomes absent from its central weekly event — “Nobody is disfellowshipped for missing church.”
- Community — Yes — Saturday observance builds an all-encompassing social world; leaving empties the calendar — “Our members are free to worship as they choose.”
- Formal membership — Mostly free — Disfellowshipping exists but is not automatic for lapse; there is no shunning requirement — “Membership is voluntary” — and on this line the claim substantially holds
- Psychological cost — Yes — Investigative-judgment scrupulosity and end-time anxiety, frequently persisting long after departure — “That is a personal matter of conscience.”
- Ministerial career — Yes — Credentials are held by conferences and can be withdrawn for doctrinal dissent — “Credentialing standards apply to everyone equally.”


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Low — The Church Manual, the 28 Fundamental Beliefs, and the Glacier View outcome are documented.
- Leadership accountability — Low — Uniquely in this codex, officers are elected in session and have been replaced by vote. This row is the tradition's strongest.
- Financial transparency — Medium — Audited and summarized at the top; hard for an individual member to trace at the level of their own congregation.
- Doctrinal discipline — Low — Credential withdrawal is a formal, recorded act with a named precedent.
- Prophetic authority — High — Formally 'lesser light,' functionally decisive — and the gap between the two is where deniability lives.
- Health teaching — Medium — Genuinely beneficial in aggregate; harms appear as individual scrupulosity, which is easy to attribute to the individual.
- Gender exclusion — Low — A recorded vote of a representative body. Nothing here is deniable, which is why this row is unusual.
- Childhood formation — High — Absorbed at home and school, attributable to no policy and no person.


### whoBenefits

- The conference and union administrative structures, whose authority over pastors runs through payroll.
- The health-system corporations and their executives, operating large revenue enterprises with governance that is intricate and rarely surfaced to members.
- The education system, which is both a genuine service and the movement's principal retention mechanism.
- The doctrinal structure itself, which rests on a claim built to be unobservable and therefore cannot be lost.


### leverage

- The hospitals, the universities, and ADRA are real, substantial, and in many places excellent. Loma Linda's longevity research is cited in mainstream science and the health message anticipated modern nutrition by a century. None of that is a cover story.
- It is nonetheless deployed as an answer to questions it does not answer. That a hospital system saves lives is not information about whether a theologian's credentials should have been withdrawn, or about what a congregation's tithe purchased.
- The parallel institution system also creates the exit cost. The same network that shelters a Sabbath-keeping minority from an indifferent world is the network a leaver has to resign from.


### whoPays

- Members who ask about the investigative judgment in a room where it is settled.
- Theologians and pastors, who hold credentials that a conference can withdraw — the tradition's real disciplinary lever.
- Women called to ministry, told by a recorded vote of a representative body that the answer is no.
- Children carrying scrupulosity from a doctrine in which their lives are under heavenly review.
- Employees in concentrated Adventist towns, for whom belief and livelihood share an address.
